12: Let us understand the Karnataka State Government's Agricultural Policy Landscape. The Karnataka state government directly shapes the agricultural environment in which an Agricultural Officer operates. Unlike central schemes, which are uniform across India, state schemes are tailored to Karnataka's specific soil types, crop patterns, and farmer demographics, and the Agricultural Officer is the primary field level implementation officer for these state schemes. The Siddaramaiah led Karnataka government, elected in 2023, made agriculture one of its focus areas, announcing the Five Guarantees, called Pancha Shakthi, of which Raitha Siri specifically targets farmers. Now, here is the Karnataka Agriculture Budget for 2025 to 26, key heads. The total agriculture department budget is over Rupees 4,500 crore, for extension, inputs, and infrastructure. The Krishi Bhagya scheme gets Rupees 800 crore, for farm ponds, watershed development, and drip irrigation. Raitha Siri, which is a PM Kisan top up, gets Rupees 500 crore, as a premium subsidy for small farmers. The PM Kisan state supplement gets Rupees 200 crore, as additional support to beneficiaries. And Bhoo Chethana, for soil and water, gets Rupees 300 crore, for soil testing and water conservation. There is also a field scenario box here, contrasting Raitha Siri with Telangana's Rythu Bandhu. A farmer asks why his cousin in Telangana gets Rupees 10,000 per acre, while he gets only Rupees 6,000 for his whole farm. The AO explains that Rythu Bandhu is calculated per acre in Telangana, while PM Kisan, which the farmer receives, is Rupees 6,000 per year per farmer family, regardless of land size, and Karnataka's Raitha Siri is a top up on PM Kisan for small and marginal farmers.
13: There is an important watch out box here. Do not confuse Karnataka's Raitha Siri with Telangana's Rythu Bandhu. They are different schemes, with different amounts and different eligibility criteria, and this is one of the most common traps in Karnataka PSC exams. There is also a quick checkpoint with two questions to test yourself. First, Karnataka's Raitha Siri scheme functions as what, on top of PM Kisan. Second, which Karnataka scheme focuses on farm pond construction and drip irrigation, Krishi Bhagya or Bhoo Chethana. The answers are given in the MCQ bank in Section 5. Now we move to Section 1.2, Central Government Schemes Affecting Farmers, starting with the five schemes every AO must know cold. These five central schemes represent the backbone of agricultural welfare in India. They appear consistently in the examination and are equally relevant during field posting. The real measure of preparation is not just whether a candidate recognises these scheme names, but whether the concepts are understood well enough to explain them clearly to a farmer encountering them for the first time. Scheme 1 is PM Kisan, direct cash with no conditions. Launched in December 2018, the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi is arguably the simplest agricultural welfare scheme India has ever run. Every landholder farmer family gets Rupees 6,000 directly into their bank account every year, in three instalments of Rupees 2,000 each, with no conditions on how they spend it. Before PM Kisan, income support always came with strings attached, but PM Kisan removed all of that, transferring money directly with no middlemen and no conditions.
14: Now let us look at the complete PM Kisan scheme profile. The full name is Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi. It was launched in December 2018. The annual amount is Rupees 6,000 per farmer family per year, given in 3 instalments of Rupees 2,000 each. The instalment schedule follows three periods, April to July, August to November, and December to March. The transfer mode is Direct Benefit Transfer, DBT, directly to the bank. Eligibility covers all landholder farmer families. Exclusions include income tax payers, government employees, and large farmers, as defined by the state. The scheme is run by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare. Karnataka coverage is around 50 lakh farmers, and the Karnataka supplement, Raitha Siri, provides a top up for small and marginal farmers. There is an important trick to remember here. Exam questions often ask about the instalment amount, Rupees 2,000, rather than the annual amount, Rupees 6,000, so know both. Also remember, PM Kisan was Rupees 6,000 from the very first instalment, it was never increased, so any option saying it was, quote, recently increased to Rupees 6,000, unquote, is wrong. A did you know box adds that PM Kisan has transferred over Rupees 3.04 lakh crore to more than 11 crore farmer families since its launch, making it one of the largest direct benefit transfer programmes in the world, with Karnataka alone having around 50 lakh beneficiary farmers. Next, students, we move to Scheme 2, PMFBY, insuring the farmer's risk, the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, launched in Kharif 2016, which replaced the old National Agricultural Insurance Scheme.
15: On this page, let us look at the complete profile of PMFBY, the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana. The key innovation of PMFBY was two fold. First, it capped the farmer's premium at a low percentage, a maximum of 2 percent for Kharif crops. Second, it brought in technology, satellite imagery and drone surveys, to assess crop damage faster and more objectively than the old committee based method. PMFBY was launched in Kharif 2016, and it replaced NAIS, the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme of 1999. The farmer premium is a maximum of 2 percent of sum insured for Kharif, 1.5 percent for Rabi, and 5 percent for horticulture. The rest of the premium is shared equally by the Centre and State governments. The coverage period runs from pre sowing to post harvest, that is 14 days after harvest. Claim technology uses satellite remote sensing plus drone surveys. In Karnataka, the State government pays 50 percent of the remaining premium, and the Raitha Suraksha scheme supplements it further. Compare this with the old NAIS of 1999. Farmer premium under NAIS was 2.5 to 3.5 percent, claim assessment was done by a village level committee, and settlement speed took months to years. Under PMFBY, settlement is targeted within 2 months. Remember, PMFBY uses the word maximum for farmer premium, so the actual premium charged can be lower than 2 percent.
16: Now, students, many exam questions try to trick you into saying the farmer always pays exactly 2 percent under PMFBY. The word maximum is the key. Also note, Rabi premium is 1.5 percent, not 2 percent, so the season matters. Let us understand this through a field conversation. A farmer says, I paid crop insurance last year and got nothing when my ragi failed, why should I pay again. The Agricultural Officer explains that under PMFBY, the scheme running now, if your crop fails due to drought, flood, or pest attack, the damage is assessed using drone surveys and satellite images. The farmer does not wait for a committee to visit the field, and the premium is a maximum of 2 percent for Kharif crops. The rest is paid by the government. The target for getting the money is within 60 days of claim submission, much faster than the old system. Two quick checkpoint questions here, which earlier scheme did PMFBY replace, and what technology does PMFBY use for claim assessment that the old NAIS did not. Next, we move to Scheme 3, the Soil Health Card. Here is a fact that surprises most people, the majority of Indian farmers apply fertilisers without ever testing their soil, following neighbours' practice or their father's habit, which wastes money and damages soil health over time. The Soil Health Card scheme was launched on 19 February 2015 by Prime Minister Modi in Suratgarh, Rajasthan, to test every farmer's soil every two years and recommend the precise fertiliser dose.
17: Here, let us go through the complete scheme profile of the Soil Health Card. It was launched on 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan. It is issued every 2 years, on a bi annual cycle. The card tests 12 parameters, namely N, P, K, pH, EC, OC, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, and B. Based on these, the card recommends fertiliser dosage for the next 3 crops specific to that farm. In Karnataka, the implementing agencies are UAS Bangalore and KSRSAC, along with District Soil Testing Labs. The significance of this scheme is that it prevents over fertilisation, saves money, and improves yield. Here is the trick to remember, if the exam gives you options of 12 parameters versus 14 parameters, choose 12. The official Soil Health Card tests 12 chemical and nutrient parameters, though some older sources mention 14 by adding physical parameters like texture and water holding capacity. The government's own documentation uses 12, so go with that. Also, watch out, do not confuse the Soil Health Card with Karnataka's own Bhoo Chethana programme, which is Karnataka's soil health and watershed conservation scheme, launched in the same year 2015 but with different implementing agencies and budgets. Did you know, India's farmers lose billions of rupees every year to over application of urea, applying 3 to 4 times more nitrogen than crops actually need. A Soil Health Card can cut fertiliser costs by 20 to 30 percent while improving yield, which is why ICAR calls it the prescription before the medicine.
18: For generations, students, India's agricultural markets worked against the farmer. A farmer in Kalaburagi who grew tur dal had only one choice, bring the produce to the nearest APMC mandi and sell to the trader present that day, at whatever price was offered, with no competition and no transparency. The electronic National Agriculture Market, called eNAM, launched in April 2016, was designed to change this power balance. By creating a single online trading platform linked to APMC mandis across India, eNAM allows buyers from anywhere in the country to bid for a farmer's produce. More buyers mean more competition, and more competition means better prices. Let us note the complete profile. The full name is Electronic National Agriculture Market. It was launched in April 2016. It is operated by the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium, abbreviated as SFAC. It works through an online portal that links APMC mandis, allowing buyers to bid from anywhere in India. In Karnataka, the State's APMC mandis are connected to the eNAM platform. Its significance is that it increases competition and improves farmer price discovery. Here is the trick to remember, the most common wrong answer for who operates eNAM is NABARD. NABARD provides rural credit, it does not operate trading platforms. SFAC, the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium, is the correct answer. If you remember nothing else about eNAM, remember this pairing, eNAM equals SFAC. Now, students, let us move to Scheme 5, the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, or RKVY, launched in 2007 to 08.
19: On this page, we learn how RKVY funds have been used in Karnataka, for farm mechanisation, cold storage construction, agri processing infrastructure, and market linkage projects. Many Farmer Producer Organisations, abbreviated FPOs, operating at the district level have received infrastructure support through RKVY allocations. Let us note the complete scheme profile. The full name is Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana. It was launched in 2007 to 08, during the 11th Five Year Plan. Its current form is called RKVY RAFTAAR, which stands for Remunerative Approaches for Agriculture and Allied Sector Rejuvenation. The funding pattern is 60 is to 40 between Centre and State, though for northeastern states it is 90 is to 10. In Karnataka, RKVY funds are used for farm mechanisation, cold storage, and Farmer Producer Organisations. Remember, RKVY was launched in 2007, not 2015 or 2016 like many newer schemes. The RAFTAAR suffix was added later during restructuring. Exam questions almost always ask about the original launch year, 2007. Two quick checkpoint questions, which organisation operates eNAM, NABARD, SFAC, FCI, or NAFED, and in which Five Year Plan was RKVY launched, the 10th, 11th, or 12th. They are necessary because 2 to 3 questions typically appear per exam. They are risky because information changes every year, and misremembering a host country or year costs you 0.75 marks in negative marking.
20: Here, students, the safest approach for international events is to learn the names and purposes of key international bodies and conferences, and memorise only the most recent host location for the most important events. Anything beyond that is risky territory. The strategy is this, for risky topics like international events, attempt a question only if you remember the specific host country and year together. If you remember only one of the two, do not attempt, because the 0.75 mark penalty is real. Let us go through the key events. COP29, the UNFCCC climate conference, was held in Baku, Azerbaijan, in November 2024, connected to carbon farming and NDC climate targets, but it is risky since it can be confused with the biodiversity COP. COP30, also UNFCCC climate, will be held in Belem, Brazil, in November 2025, connected to food and agriculture tracks, and this is especially risky as it is the most recent event before the July 2026 exam. CBD COP16, the biodiversity conference, was held in Cali, Colombia, in October 2024, connected to the 30 by 30 target and Western Ghats implementation, and it is risky due to confusion with the climate COP. The G20 Agriculture Ministers meeting for 2025 was hosted in South Africa. 21: On this page, we learn that COP30 at Belem, Brazil, in November 2025, is significant for agriculture because Brazil chairs the event as the world's largest agricultural exporter, and the Amazon and tropical forest agriculture connection is the defining agenda item. The Kunming Montreal 30 by 30 target, to protect 30 percent of land and ocean by 2030, is monitored through these COP conferences. Now, students, we move to section 1.4, Important Appointments in the Agricultural Sector. Appointment questions are a classic exam gamble, because people retire, resign, and get replaced, so a fact that was correct in January may be wrong by July. For the 2026 exam, you need to verify appointment names in the two weeks before the exam from official government websites. What you can safely learn, and what will not change, is the role and significance of each institution, since the person in the chair changes but the chair itself does not. Let us go through the key institutions. ICAR, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, conducts agri research and releases crop varieties, and matters to an AO because varieties recommended to farmers come from ICAR. NABARD, the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development, is the apex rural credit institution and refinances banks, relevant for Kisan Credit Card loans and SHG credit. FCI, the Food Corporation of India, procures food grains at minimum support price and manages buffer stock, relevant because farmers bring produce and the AO facilitates MSP procurement. SFAC, the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium, operates eNAM and promotes agribusiness for small farmers.
22: Here, students, is one appointment fact that rarely changes and is frequently tested. The Director General of ICAR also serves as the Secretary of DARE, the Department of Agricultural Research and Education. One person holds both titles simultaneously, and this dual role fact appears in almost every Karnataka PSC agriculture exam. Before the exam, verify these appointments two weeks in advance, since names change but the book gives you where to check. Check the Director General of ICAR, who is also Secretary of DARE, at icar.org.in. Check the Chairman and Managing Director of NABARD at nabard.org. A useful tip is to search the institution name followed by head 2026 on Google and check the official site for the current name. Now we move to section 1.5, Awards and Recognitions in Agriculture. Agricultural awards tell you which practices the government endorses, which states lead in production, and which scientists have contributed to Indian farming. These are stable facts, they do not change year to year the way appointments do, so learn them once and they stay with you. The Krishi Karman Award is given by the Government of India, Ministry of Agriculture, for best performing states in food grain production by category, and Karnataka has won it for rice and coarse cereals. The National Agriculture Award covers best farmer, best ATMA, and best KVK districts.
23: On this page, let us finish the awards table and learn about the World Food Prize and Padma awards. The World Food Prize is given by the World Food Prize Foundation, for global contribution to food security, and it is called the Nobel of Food, but it is NOT given by the Nobel Committee. The Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan awards are given by the Government of India for contribution across all fields including agriculture, and Subhash Palekar received the Padma Shri in 2016 for Zero Budget Natural Farming. Here is the trick to remember, the World Food Prize is universally called the Nobel Prize for Food and Agriculture. The trap is that it is NOT given by the Nobel Committee, it is given by the World Food Prize Foundation. A Nobel Prize for Agriculture simply does not exist, so if you see that phrase as an answer option, it is always wrong. Now, students, let us understand Zero Budget Natural Farming, abbreviated ZBNF, promoted by Subhash Palekar and officially adopted by Karnataka. It is a farming system where the farmer does not spend any money on external inputs, and all inputs come from on farm resources, cow dung, cow urine, local plants, and fermentation products. Karnataka adopted this approach because chemical input costs had become the single largest burden on small farmers. Did you know, ZBNF has four core components. Beejamrit is seed treatment with cow dung water. Jiwamrit is a soil inoculant made from cow dung, cow urine, jaggery, and pulse flour. Mulching means covering crop residue over soil. And Waaphasa means maintaining soil moisture air balance. Expect one MCQ testing these component names with their functions.
24: Now, students, let us move to section 1.6, Key Budgetary Allocations in the Union Budget 2025 to 26. The Union Budget is the government's annual statement of priorities, and in agriculture, budget allocations indicate which schemes will receive active implementation focus during the year. The Union Budget 2025 to 26 made two things clear, income support through PM Kisan remains the government's largest agricultural commitment, and natural farming has moved from a pilot initiative to a full national mission. PM Kisan received an allocation of 63,500 crore rupees, the largest single agri scheme, and as an AO you will verify beneficiary lists. PMFBY, the crop insurance scheme, received 14,600 crore rupees, used for premium subsidy and enrolment drives at the district level. RKVY, the state infrastructure scheme, received 7,100 crore rupees, accessed at the district level for infrastructure funding. The National Mission on Natural Farming is a new scheme with 2,481 crore rupees, and the ZBNF extension is now part of the AO's mandate. The total Agriculture Ministry budget is approximately 1.52 lakh crore rupees, covering the overall envelope. Let us look closer at the National Mission on Natural Farming, abbreviated NMNF. It received 2,481 crore rupees in Budget 2025 to 26 and represents the most important new scheme for AOs in the upcoming exam. Beyond the budget figure, understand the scheme's architecture, since this is what exam questions will test.
25: Here is the full scheme structure of the National Mission on Natural Farming. The budget allocation is 2,481 crore rupees under Union Budget 2025 to 26. The farmer coverage target is 1 crore farmers across India. The cluster approach covers 15,000 clusters, with one cluster per village panchayat group. The nodal research agency is ICAR NRRI, the National Rice Research Institute at Cuttack. The implementing agency is the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare. The basis of this mission is Subhash Palekar's ZBNF four component system. The four ZBNF components are Beejamrit for seed, Jiwamrit for soil, Mulching, and Waaphasa for aeration. In Karnataka, this is especially relevant since Karnataka was an early adopter of ZBNF, and state NMNF clusters were prioritised. Here is the trick, the exam may ask, which institute is the nodal agency for NMNF, and the answer is ICAR NRRI, the National Rice Research Institute, Cuttack. Do not confuse this with ICAR NAARM, the National Academy of Agricultural Research Management, or IARI in New Delhi. NRRI is specifically for natural farming research. Watch out, Karnataka Budget 2026 to 27 was tabled in February or March 2026, after the figures in this book were prepared, so since the exam is in July 2026, budget 2026 to 27 figures may be tested. Verify the current year's allocation from finance.kar.nic.in one week before the exam. Now we move to section 1.7, Karnataka GI Tags and APEDA, agricultural exports. A Geographical Indication, or GI tag, is a legal identity for a product that originates from a specific geographic region and possesses qualities attributable to that origin.
26: On this page, let us understand why GI tags matter to an Agricultural Officer. For Karnataka's farmers, GI tags mean higher prices, protected branding, and access to international markets. GI tags are not just policy knowledge, they are a market promotion tool. When a farmer in Nanjangud grows bananas, an AO who knows the GI tag can direct that farmer to marketing channels that command the GI premium. Questions on GI tags appear 1 to 2 times per Karnataka PSC agriculture exam, and they are reliable safe questions because the facts are stable. AOs in GI tagged crop districts actively participate in marketing, verifying production methods, helping farmers register with APEDA export channels, and organising collective branding, which is direct field relevance for Kodagu, Mandya, Dharwad, and Udupi posted AOs. Now let us learn about APEDA, the export promotion body for agri products. The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority, APEDA, was established in 1986 under the APEDA Act, 1985. It operates under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not the Ministry of Agriculture, and this distinction matters because exam options frequently list Agriculture Ministry as a trap. APEDA's mandate is to promote exports of scheduled agricultural and processed food products. It registers exporters, sets quality standards, promotes GI tagged products internationally, and provides financial assistance to agri exporters. For Karnataka, APEDA connects Coorg coffee, Mysore silk, and Nanjangud banana producers to global markets. Note its establishment year 1986 under the APEDA Act of 1985, its ministry, mandate, and key functions.
27: Here, students, note that APEDA's headquarters is in New Delhi, and the Karnataka products it promotes include Coorg Arabica coffee, Mysore silk, Nanjangud banana, and Dharwad pedha. Now let us understand the legal framework, the Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999. GI tags in India are governed by this Act, which came into force in 2003 and is administered by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. A GI tag protects a product's geographic origin claim for an initial period of 10 years, renewable, and unauthorised use of a registered GI is a punishable offence. Karnataka has been aggressive in registering its traditional products, and the state has one of the highest concentrations of registered GI tags in India. Let us go through Karnataka's GI tagged products. Coorg Arabica Coffee, also called Kodagu Arabica, from Kodagu district, is grown at high altitude of 900 to 1600 metres, shade grown, single origin premium coffee, and it is safe since Kodagu coffee equals GI equals APEDA export. Mysore Silk, or Mysuru Silk, from Mysuru district, is pure mulberry silk, KSIC produced, with a specific weave pattern, and it is the most famous Karnataka GI tag. Nanjangud Banana, or Nanjangude Rasabale, from Nanjangud in Mysuru district, has a unique flavour due to specific soil and water of the Nanjangud river belt, and it is the only banana in Karnataka with GI status. 48: Let us continue the SI Units table, students. Electric current is measured in Amperes, relevant to motor current in irrigation pumps. 49: On this page, students, we move into section 2.2, Chemistry, covering soil pH, acids, bases, and fertiliser composition. Chemistry is the most directly relevant science for an Agricultural Officer, since every soil test result is a chemical reading. We then examine Karnataka Soil pH Profiles. Red soils of North Karnataka have pH 5.5 to 6.5 and are acidic due to leaching, needing lime if below 5.5. Black cotton soils of Central Karnataka have pH 7.5 to 8.5, alkaline, with common iron and manganese deficiency. Laterite soils of Coastal and Malnad regions have pH 4.5 to 5.5, strongly acidic, needing lime before planting. Alluvial soils of river plains have pH 6.5 to 7.5, near neutral, and are most productive for diverse crops. Remember, link soil type to corrective measure, lime for acidic soils, gypsum for alkaline soils. The page closes with a field example from Kolar, where a farmer's soil at pH 5.2 is acidic, and the Agricultural Officer explains that nitrogen in urea converts to gas and escapes before roots can absorb it.
50: Now, students, the Agricultural Officer's advice continues, agricultural lime, about 500 kilograms per acre, should be applied to raise pH to around 6.5, and urea should be applied only after waiting two weeks. Next comes the Major Fertilisers table, showing composition and field use. Urea has 46 percent nitrogen, the highest nitrogen content of all solid fertilisers. DAP has 18 percent nitrogen and 46 percent phosphate, the most popular phosphatic fertiliser in India. MOP has 60 percent potash, the only major potassic fertiliser. SSP has 16 percent phosphate and also supplies 11 percent sulphur, an advantage over DAP. Ammonium Sulphate has 21 percent nitrogen and also supplies 24 percent sulphur, good for alkaline soils. Nano Urea from IFFCO is about 4 percent liquid nitrogen, a foliar spray launched in 2021, where 500 millilitres equals one 45 kilogram bag. Nano DAP from IFFCO is about 8 percent liquid phosphate, used for seed treatment and foliar application, launched in 2023. Remember the trick, Urea equals 46 percent nitrogen, DAP equals 18 nitrogen plus 46 phosphate, MOP equals 60 percent potash, and SSP equals 16 phosphate plus 11 sulphur. These four numbers appear in almost every General Science paper. The page then begins the Micronutrients and Deficiency Symptoms table with zinc.
51: Let us understand the Micronutrients and Deficiency Symptoms table, students. Zinc deficiency causes white bud, a condition of pale, stunted new leaves, most common in paddy and maize in South Karnataka, corrected with zinc sulphate at 25 kilograms per hectare. Boron deficiency causes hollow heart in groundnut and tip burn in sugarcane, reported in groundnut belts of Kalaburagi, corrected with borax foliar spray at 0.2 percent. Iron deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis, where leaves yellow but veins stay green, occurring in alkaline black soils of North Karnataka that lock up iron, corrected with ferrous sulphate foliar spray. Manganese deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis similar to iron but affecting mid-leaves, occurring in high pH soils, corrected with manganese sulphate spray. Copper deficiency causes blue-green leaf tip dieback and poor grain filling, less common, found in coastal paddy areas, corrected with copper sulphate application. Next, we begin the Biofertilisers table. Rhizobium, a bacteria, fixes atmospheric nitrogen in legume root nodules, applied to pulses like tur, chana, soybean, and groundnut. Azospirillum, also bacteria, is free-living, fixes nitrogen, and promotes root growth in cereals like rice, maize, wheat, and sorghum.
52: On this page, students, the Biofertilisers table continues. PSB, meaning Bacillus or Pseudomonas, converts insoluble soil phosphorus into plant-available form, useful for all crops in high-phosphorus-locked soils. VAM, a fungi, extends root surface area and improves phosphorus and zinc uptake, useful for fruit crops, vegetables, and plantation crops. Azolla, a fern-cyanobacteria symbiosis, fixes nitrogen as green manure in rice, widely used in Karnataka's rice tracts. An Agri Lens box notes that Karnataka's Department of Agriculture provides Rhizobium and Azospirillum cultures at subsidised rates through Raitha Samparka Kendras. We then move into section 2.3, Biology, covering Cell Structure, Photosynthesis, and Plant Reproduction. The Cell Structure comparison table begins, showing that plant cells have a cellulose cell wall giving rigidity and determining crop straw quality, while animal cells lack a cell wall. Plant cells have chloroplasts, the site of photosynthesis, absent in animal cells and absent in roots. Plant cells have a large central vacuole, up to 90 percent of cell volume, storing water, pigments, and waste, while animal cells have small, multiple vacuoles.
53: Now, students, we look at the photosynthesis equation, 6 CO2 plus 6 H2O plus light energy yields C6H12O6, glucose, plus 6 O2. The Photosynthesis Pathways table follows. The C3 or Calvin Cycle pathway fixes CO2 directly by an enzyme called RuBisCO, is efficient in cool, moist conditions, and applies to wheat, rice, cotton, and most legumes, relevant to rice in the Kaveri command area which needs good water supply. The C4, or Hatch-Slack pathway, concentrates CO2 before the Calvin Cycle, is efficient in hot, dry conditions, and applies to maize, sugarcane, jowar, and bajra, relevant to jowar in North Karnataka, a drought-tolerant, dry-zone crop. The CAM pathway opens stomata at night, fixing CO2 then to save water, applying to pineapple and agave, of minor relevance in extreme drought crops. Remember, C3 means rice, wheat, cotton, and C4 means maize, sugarcane, jowar, bajra, with C4 crops needing less water per unit of biomass. Next, the Vegetative Propagation table begins, covering cutting, where a stem or leaf section is planted in soil, simple with no special equipment, used for rose, sugarcane, and cassava, and grafting, where a shoot, called the scion, is joined to a rooted rootstock, combining disease resistance with high yield, used for mango, citrus, and sapota.
54: Let us finish the Vegetative Propagation table, students. Budding involves inserting a single bud into a rootstock, using less scion material for fast, reliable results, applied to rose, rubber, and cashew. Layering bends a branch to the ground and roots it while still attached, giving high success rate, used for lychee, jasmine, and guava. Tissue culture multiplies cells in a sterile lab medium for large-scale multiplication, giving disease-free plants, used for banana, sugarcane, potato, and cardamom. Now, students, we move into section 2.3a, Photoperiodism and Vernalisation. Photoperiodism is a plant's response to the relative length of day and night in a 24-hour cycle, and flowering time in many crops is controlled purely by hours of light and darkness, not temperature or nutrients. This is critical for crop planning, since the same variety planted in the wrong season will fail to flower regardless of water or fertiliser applied. The table shows Short-Day Plants, requiring night length longer than a critical dark period, under 12 hours of daylight, including jowar, rice, sugarcane at initiation, and bajra, flowering October to November in Karnataka. Long-Day Plants require night length shorter than critical, over 12 hours of daylight, including wheat, barley, spinach, and mustard, flowering in winter months when extended daylight is needed, though this is limited in Karnataka.
55: On this page, we finish the photoperiodism table and move into vernalisation. Quick recap first. Short-day plants, or SDP, include jowar, rice, onion, bajra, and sugarcane for flowering, they flower when nights are long. Long-day plants, LDP, are wheat, barley, spinach, mustard, and oat. Day-neutral plants, DNP, flower regardless of day length, triggered instead by age or temperature, and these include tomato, cotton, maize, sunflower, and buckwheat. Here is the exam trick. Short-day means flowers when nights are long, think of it as short day equals long night equals the winter or monsoon transition. Remember jowar and rice as SDP, wheat as LDP, and tomato, cotton, maize as DNP, these seven crop mappings cover most expected questions. Did you know that the terms short-day and long-day are actually scientifically misleading, because what really matters is the length of the night, not the day. Short-day plants are technically long-night plants, and the pigment phytochrome senses night length. Karnataka's jowar flowers in October to November precisely because nights become long enough after September. Then we begin vernalisation, the process where a plant is exposed to prolonged cold to induce or speed up flowering, evolved so winter crops do not flower before winter arrives. Wheat is the classic vernalisation example, needing 6 to 8 weeks at 1 to 7 degrees Celsius.
56: Let us understand vernalisation and then move to nutrition. The table confirms wheat, especially winter varieties, needs 6 to 8 weeks of cold at 1 to 7 degrees Celsius to flower. In Karnataka, this has an important implication, since winters are not cold enough for vernalisation, Karnataka grows spring wheat instead, which does not need vernalisation. This is marked as a safe exam fact, stable and non-changing, worth 1 to 2 marks. The Agri Lens box explains why this matters practically. When an Agricultural Officer introduces a new rice or jowar variety to a farmer, the variety's photoperiod sensitivity determines when it will flower. Day-neutral, photo-insensitive varieties are preferred for modern farming because they can be planted in any season, which is why improved jowar varieties developed by UAS Dharwad were selected for photoperiod insensitivity, enabling double cropping. Two quick checkpoint questions follow, on which months jowar typically flowers in Karnataka, and what vernalisation means and why winter wheat is uncommon there. Now, students, we move to a new topic, section 2.4, nutrition, covering macronutrients, micronutrients, and deficiency diseases. This section covers both human nutrition for public health scheme questions and the scientific basis of food composition, especially caloric values of macronutrients, vitamin classification, and deficiency diseases. The macronutrient table begins with carbohydrates, giving 4 kilocalories per gram, sourced from grains, tubers, and fruits, with ragi, rice, and jowar as Karnataka examples, and proteins, also 4 kilocalories per gram, from pulses, meat, eggs, and dairy, with tur dal, horse gram, and groundnut as examples.
57: Here on this page we complete the macronutrient table and study vitamins in detail. Fats provide 9 kilocalories per gram, the highest of the three, sourced from oils, nuts, and dairy fat, with groundnut oil, sunflower oil, and coconut oil as Karnataka examples. Here is the trick to remember this. Carbohydrates equal 4, proteins equal 4, fats equal 9, so carbs and proteins are both 4, while fats are 9, more than double. Next comes the vitamins table, dividing them into fat-soluble and water-soluble types. Fat-soluble vitamins are A or retinol, causing night blindness and xerophthalmia if deficient, sourced from carrots, green leafy vegetables, and mango. Vitamin D or cholecalciferol causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, sourced from sunlight, fish oil, and egg yolk. Vitamin E or tocopherol causes infertility and muscle weakness, found in wheat germ oil, sunflower oil, and nuts. Vitamin K or phylloquinone causes poor blood clotting and excessive bleeding, found in green vegetables and liver. Water-soluble vitamins include B1 or thiamine, causing beriberi, B3 or niacin, causing pellagra, B12 or cobalamin, causing pernicious anaemia, and vitamin C or ascorbic acid, causing scurvy, found in citrus fruits, amla, and guava. The trick here, fat-soluble vitamins spell A D E K, remembered as, a doctor examines kids. Finally, Karnataka's mid-day meal scheme uses ragi, finger millet, which has the highest calcium of any grain, 344 milligrams per 100 grams, more iron than rice or wheat, and is rich in amino acids.
58: Now, students, this page opens section 2.5, health, covering diseases, vaccines, and public health programmes. The Agri Lens box first reminds us Karnataka is India's largest producer of ragi, a drought-tolerant crop growing well on red laterite soils with rainfall as low as 700 millimetres, central to food security in dryland tracts. Two checkpoint questions ask about the vitamin deficiency causing pellagra and its three symptoms, and three nutritional advantages of ragi over polished rice. Health questions in the AO or AAO exam focus on disease classification, vectors, vaccines, and public health scheme names. Disease names and causative organisms are factual and stable, but specific current figures change frequently and should be verified before the exam. A strategy box advises attempting questions on disease classification, causative organisms, and vaccines confidently since these facts are stable, but avoiding guesses on specific budgetary allocations or newly launched sub-schemes, especially since the penalty of minus 0.75 for wrong answers is significant. The classification of diseases table begins. Bacterial diseases, caused by bacteria, include tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, and plague, transmitted by droplets for TB, water for cholera and typhoid, and fleas for plague. Viral diseases include dengue, influenza, polio, hepatitis B, and rabies, transmitted by Aedes mosquito for dengue, droplets for flu, and faecal-oral route for polio. Protozoan diseases include malaria and kala-azar, transmitted by Anopheles mosquito and sandfly respectively. Fungal diseases include ringworm, candidiasis, and aspergillosis, spread by contact or spore inhalation.
59: On this page we complete the disease classification table and move into vaccines. Helminthic diseases, caused by worms, include filariasis, ascariasis, and tapeworm, transmitted by Culex mosquito for filariasis or contaminated food and water for the others. Remember this key distinction, malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan, carried by the female Anopheles mosquito, while dengue is caused by a virus, carried by Aedes aegypti, both are mosquito-borne but belong to entirely different disease categories. Next we study India's Universal Immunisation Programme, or UIP, which provides free vaccines to children against 12 preventable diseases. The complete schedule table lists each vaccine, disease prevented, route of administration, and timing. BCG protects against tuberculosis, given intra-dermally in the left arm at birth. OPV, oral polio vaccine, protects against poliomyelitis via oral drops, given at birth, 6, 10, and 14 weeks, with boosters at 16 to 24 months. Hepatitis B vaccine is intramuscular, given at birth, 6, 10, and 14 weeks. DPT protects against diphtheria, pertussis or whooping cough, and tetanus, intramuscular, given at 6, 10, 14 weeks with a booster at 16 to 24 months. Rotavirus vaccine, given orally at 6, 10, and 14 weeks, protects against rotavirus gastroenteritis or diarrhoea. PCV, the pneumococcal vaccine, is intramuscular, protecting against pneumonia and meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, given at 6 and 14 weeks with a booster at 9 to 12 months. The fIPV, inactivated polio vaccine, is intra-dermal, given at 14 weeks and 6 months. Measles or MR vaccine is subcutaneous, given at 9 to 12 months with a booster at 15 to 18 months.
60: Let us continue the vaccine schedule and then look at Karnataka's disease burden. JE vaccine, for Japanese Encephalitis, is subcutaneous, given at 9 to 12 months, but only in endemic districts. The DPT booster is given again at 5 to 6 years, school age. Here is the trick examiners love to test, two vaccines added recently to the UIP. First, the Rotavirus vaccine, for diarrhoea, given orally at 6, 10, and 14 weeks. Second, PCV, for pneumonia and meningitis, given at 6 and 14 weeks plus a booster. These are the new additions that distinguish a well-prepared candidate. Now, students, we look at Karnataka-specific disease burden. Dengue is active with increasing urban cases, seasonal from July to November, most affected districts being Bengaluru Urban, Dakshina Kannada, Udupi, and Mysuru. Malaria is coastal-endemic, with Plasmodium falciparum dominating the coastal belt, affecting Uttara Kannada, Udupi, and Dakshina Kannada. Kala-azar has free status in Karnataka, meaning the state has eliminated visceral leishmaniasis, no endemic districts, and this is relevant as a negative fact in exams. Japanese Encephalitis has endemic pockets in Mysuru, Mandya, Ramanagara, and Kalaburagi, with targeted vaccination there. Scrub Typhus is emerging, linked to agricultural field exposure, in Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru, and Shivamogga forest margins. Did you know, Karnataka achieved kala-azar free status, meaning it has eliminated visceral leishmaniasis as a public health problem. Exam questions sometimes include kala-azar in options for diseases prevalent in Karnataka as a trap, remember, Karnataka is kala-azar free.
61: Here we study public health programmes specific to Karnataka. Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY provides rupees 5 lakh per year per family for hospitalisation, and in Karnataka it is combined with Arogya Karnataka for expanded coverage. Arogya Karnataka is the state extension with no income cap, covering middle-income families too. Janani Suraksha Yojana, JSY, gives a cash incentive for institutional delivery, with high beneficiary counts in North Karnataka districts. POSHAN Abhiyaan addresses stunting, wasting, and anaemia in children under six, run in Karnataka under the ICDS programme umbrella. A watch-out box clarifies that Ayushman Bharat has two components, PM-JAY, the rupees 5 lakh insurance scheme, and Health and Wellness Centres, HWCs. The rupees 5 lakh insurance figure is safe to remember, but specific beneficiary counts are risky to guess. Two checkpoint questions ask which mosquito transmits malaria and which transmits dengue, and to name two vaccines recently added to India's UIP schedule. Now, students, a new topic begins, section 2.5a, irrigation water quality, covering electrical conductivity, pH, and SAR. Irrigation water is not just H2O, canal water, borewell water, and tank water all carry dissolved salts, which accumulate in the soil through repeated irrigation and evaporation.
62: Let us understand why water quality matters so much for irrigation. When dissolved salts accumulate in soil through repeated irrigation and evaporation, they can damage soil structure, reduce crop yield, and eventually make land uncultivable. The three key parameters for assessing irrigation water quality are Electrical Conductivity, EC, pH, and the Sodium Absorption Ratio, SAR. An Agricultural Officer in North Karnataka's canal command areas, such as Raichur, Vijayapura, and Yadgir, deals with these irrigation water quality problems regularly, so this is both exam and field knowledge. Parameter one is EC, which measures the total dissolved salts in water. Pure water does not conduct electricity, salts make it conductive, so higher EC means more dissolved salts and more potential for soil salinity damage. The EC thresholds table shows, EC below 0.75 dS per metre, roughly 250 microsiemens per centimetre, is safe for all crops and soils, low salinity hazard. EC between 0.75 and 1.5 is moderate hazard, safe for tolerant crops but needs monitoring. EC between 1.5 and 3.0 is high hazard, suitable only for salt-tolerant crops like cotton, barley, and sugarcane, with leaching needed. EC above 3.0 is harmful, unsuitable for most crops, restricting root water uptake. Note, 1 dS per metre equals 1 mmhos per centimetre, approximately 640 milligrams per litre of total dissolved solids. Parameter two is pH, with the ideal irrigation range being 6.5 to 8.4. Parameter three is SAR, sodium absorption ratio, measuring sodium relative to calcium and magnesium, high sodium disperses soil particles, forming a hardpan or sodic soil.
63: On this page we look closely at SAR and crop tolerance to salinity. The formula for SAR is sodium ion divided by the square root of calcium ion plus magnesium ion, all divided by two, with concentrations measured in milliequivalents per litre. This is described as a serious long-term water quality problem specifically in North Karnataka's black cotton soil areas. The SAR value table shows, SAR below 10 is low hazard, safe for all soils, suitable for all crops including vegetables. SAR 10 to 18 is medium hazard, causing minor dispersion in fine soils, requiring monitoring, tolerant field crops only, avoid vegetables. SAR 18 to 26 is high hazard, causing significant soil dispersion and poor drainage, use with caution, only most tolerant crops with soil amendment. SAR above 26 is very high hazard, causing severe soil structure damage and waterlogging, not suitable for agriculture at all. A second table lists crop EC tolerance thresholds. Bean, pea, and carrot are very sensitive, below 1.0 dS per metre. Groundnut, maize, and potato are moderately sensitive, 1.0 to 2.0. Wheat, jowar, and tomato are moderately tolerant, 2.0 to 4.0. Cotton and barley are tolerant, selected for saline soils, 4.0 to 8.0. Sugarcane, Karnataka's major irrigated crop, tolerates a moderate range of 1.7 to 3.0. The trick to remember, EC below 0.75 is safe for all crops, EC above 3.0 is harmful for most, SAR below 10 is low hazard, SAR above 26 is very high, avoid use, these four numbers are the complete exam answer bank for irrigation water quality questions.
64: Let us finish the irrigation water topic and move into pesticides. A did-you-know box explains Karnataka's Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal command area, in Raichur and Koppal districts, has significant soil salinity problems from years of irrigation with high-EC water from the Krishna river system, requiring annual soil testing and regular leaching, a direct field responsibility of Agricultural Officers posted there. Two checkpoint questions ask the maximum safe EC for unrestricted irrigation, and what a high SAR value indicates, high calcium, high sodium, or high phosphorus hazard. Now, students, a new topic opens, section 2.6, pesticide classification and safety. Agricultural Officers are legally responsible for overseeing safe pesticide use in their jurisdiction. An AO must be able to read a pesticide label, recognise the hazard class, advise farmers on safe application, and enforce the Pre-Harvest Interval rule. Questions on pesticide classification are rated safe, since the classification system is well-defined and stable. The WHO toxicity classification uses a colour-coded label system. The World Health Organization classifies pesticides by oral and dermal toxicity, and India's Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee, CIB and RC, uses this WHO classification for mandatory colour-coded labels on all registered pesticides, so even illiterate farmers can judge relative hazard from the label colour. The table begins, Class Ia, extremely hazardous, red label with a skull and crossbones symbol, LD50 below 5 milligrams per kilogram, examples parathion, phorate, and carbofuran. Class Ib, highly hazardous, red label, LD50 5 to 50, examples monocrotophos, methyl parathion, and endosulfan, which is banned. Class II, moderately hazardous, yellow label, LD50 50 to 2000, examples chlorpyrifos, dichlorvos, and lambda-cyhalothrin.
65: On this page we complete the WHO pesticide classification and study key regulatory concepts. Class III, slightly hazardous, blue label, LD50 2000 to 5000, examples glyphosate, malathion, and captan. Class U, unlikely hazardous, green label, LD50 above 5000, examples Bt spray, Bacillus thuringiensis, and copper sulphate. Here is the trick, remember the label colour mnemonic, red means danger, like a red traffic light, stop, very hazardous, yellow means caution, slow down, blue means careful, and green means generally safe. The colour change from red to green tracks decreasing hazard, and Class Ia and Ib both have red labels, distinguished by the skull symbol which only Class Ia always has. Two regulatory concepts are tested repeatedly and are directly relevant to field work. PHI, Pre-Harvest Interval, means the minimum number of days between the last pesticide application and harvest, essential for food safety and export compliance. For example, chlorpyrifos on tomato requires 7 days with no harvesting after the last spray, while lambda-cyhalothrin on cotton requires 14 days, relevant for Bt cotton and insecticide scenarios in Karnataka. Banned pesticides in India include Endosulfan, banned by Supreme Court order in 2011, DDT, banned for agricultural use, BHC or HCH, Aldrin, and Dieldrin. Endosulfan was banned following the Kasaragod tragedy in Kerala, where aerial spraying caused neurological damage to children in cashew plantations near the Karnataka border. CIB and RC is the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee, which registers all pesticides in India under the Ministry of Agriculture. A watch-out box stresses that endosulfan is completely banned, not just restricted, so any exam option calling it available with restrictions is wrong.
66: Let us look at a practical field training dialogue on pesticide label reading. An AO explains to farmers before distributing pesticide bags, asking what colour stripe is at the bottom of the bag. One farmer answers yellow, and the AO explains yellow means Class II, moderately hazardous, in this case chlorpyrifos, requiring gloves and a mask during application, with a printed PHI of 7 days, meaning vegetables must not be harvested for 7 days after the last spray, otherwise pesticide residue remains in the food. Another farmer asks what a red stripe would mean, and the AO explains red indicates Class Ia or Ib, extremely or highly hazardous, and as an AO, only Class Ib pesticides can be authorised for licensed applicators with proper protective equipment, while Class Ia pesticides are mostly banned or restricted, and any product with a green stripe is the safest choice to use whenever effective. A did-you-know box reinforces that India banned Endosulfan in 2011 after the Supreme Court order, and Karnataka's Kodagu district was also affected by endosulfan use on coffee plantations in the late 1990s and 2000s, after which the state government restricted several organophosphate pesticides in certain districts following field health studies. As an AO, knowledge of the current banned and restricted pesticide list is a legal requirement. Two checkpoint questions ask for the WHO class and label colour of a moderately hazardous pesticide, and to define PHI and explain why it matters for food safety in horticulture crops. 70: Now, students, we begin Practice Questions for this unit, a set of 28 questions total, each with a strategy note, followed by the answer, the reasoning, and the most common trap to avoid. Question 1, marked safe to attempt, asks which fertiliser has the highest percentage of nitrogen among solid fertilisers, options being Ammonium Sulphate at 21 percent, DAP at 18 percent, Urea at 46 percent, or SSP at 16 percent P2O5. The correct answer is Urea, 46 percent nitrogen, because it contains the highest concentration of nitrogen among all solid fertilisers and is the most widely used nitrogenous fertiliser in India and Karnataka. The trap to avoid is assuming DAP has the highest nitrogen since it's popular, but DAP has only 18 percent nitrogen, its strength being in phosphorus at 46 percent P2O5, not nitrogen. Question 2, also safe to attempt, asks the pH range of black cotton soils found in Central Karnataka, with options from 4.5 up to 8.5. The correct answer is 7.5 to 8.5, because black cotton soils, called Vertisols, in Karnataka are alkaline, heavy, clay-rich soils that swell when wet and crack when dry. The trap to avoid is confusing black soil, which is alkaline, with red soil, which is acidic at 5.5 to 6.5, or laterite soil, which is even more acidic, this soil-type mix-up is the most common error. Question 3 begins, asking which group of crops has Rhizobium bacteria fixing atmospheric nitrogen in their root nodules, with the answer options starting with cereals like rice, wheat, and maize.
71: Let us continue with question 3's answer, and then work through questions 4, 5, and the start of 6. Question 3's correct answer is legumes such as tur, groundnut, and soybean, because Rhizobium forms a symbiotic relationship specifically with legume roots, entering root hairs and forming nodules where nitrogen fixation occurs. The trap to avoid is confusing this with Azospirillum, which works with cereals like rice, maize, and wheat, Rhizobium is exclusively a legume symbiont. Question 4, safe to attempt, asks the caloric value of dietary fat per gram, options 4, 7, 9, or 11 kilocalories. The correct answer is 9 kilocalories, more than double the 4 kilocalories per gram provided by both carbohydrates and proteins. The trap to avoid is guessing 7 kilocalories as a middle value between 4 and 9, but 7 is not a standard caloric value for any macronutrient, the answer is always 9 for fat. Question 5, safe to attempt, asks which vitamins are classified as fat-soluble. The correct answer is vitamins A, D, E, and K, remembered as ADEK, since these four dissolve in fats and are stored in body fat and the liver. The trap to avoid is confusing which group includes vitamin D, since vitamins B and C are actually water-soluble, and vitamin D is fat-soluble as part of ADEK. Question 6, safe to attempt, begins, asking which class of lever the hoe or kudali used in farming represents, with option A being Class 1, fulcrum between effort and load.
72: On this page we finish question 6 and work through questions 7 and the start of 8. Question 6's correct answer is Class 3, where effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. In a hoe, the hands apply effort at the middle of the handle, the tip, or load, moves soil at one end, and the wrist acts as fulcrum, so effort in the middle equals Class 3. The trap to avoid is assuming a long-handled tool is automatically Class 1, but the distinguishing factor is where the effort is applied, not the tool's length. Question 7, safe to attempt, asks about jowar or sorghum, categorised as a C4 plant, and what is the primary advantage of C4 photosynthesis for crops in dryland Karnataka. The correct answer is that C4 plants lose less water per unit of carbon fixed and tolerate high temperatures better. This is because C4 plants concentrate CO2 before the Calvin Cycle, making photosynthesis more efficient under hot, dry conditions, reducing water loss per unit of biomass produced. The trap to avoid is thinking C4 is about root depth or nitrogen independence, but the correct advantage is water-use efficiency, not those factors. Question 8, safe to attempt, begins, asking why ragi or finger millet is nutritionally significant in Karnataka, with the correct answer already marked as calcium, the highest of any cereal grain, while option D, protein more than wheat, is a trap since ragi's protein at 7 to 8 percent is comparable to, not higher than, wheat's roughly 12 percent.
73: Let us complete question 8 and work through questions 9, 10, and the start of 11. Question 8's correct answer is calcium, the highest of any cereal grain, since ragi contains approximately 344 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, far higher than rice's roughly 10 milligrams or wheat's roughly 41 milligrams, making it important for combating bone deficiency. The trap to avoid is assuming ragi's protein content, about 7 to 8 percent, is higher than wheat's, about 12 percent, when it is actually comparable, not higher. Question 9, safe to attempt, asks in which year IFFCO's Nano Urea was launched, and its primary mode of application. The correct answer is 2021, applied as a foliar spray on leaves. IFFCO commercially launched Nano Urea in 2021 as a liquid formulation sprayed directly onto crop leaves, with one 500 millilitre bottle claimed to replace one 45 kilogram bag of conventional urea. The trap to avoid is confusing this with Nano DAP, a 2023 innovation, since Nano Urea is foliar, not soil-applied. Question 10, safe to attempt, asks which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness. The correct answer is vitamin A, since retinol is essential for producing rhodopsin, the visual pigment in rod cells, and without it, rhodopsin cannot regenerate, causing difficulty seeing in dim light. The trap to avoid is vitamin D, which causes rickets, a bone disease, not vision problems, night blindness is a core vitamin A fact. Question 11, safe to attempt, begins, asking which mosquito species transmits malaria and which transmits dengue.
74: On this page we finish question 11 and work through questions 12, 13, and the start of 14. Question 11's correct answer is that the female Anopheles mosquito transmits malaria, carrying Plasmodium, while Aedes aegypti transmits the dengue virus. The trap to avoid is that Culex mosquito transmits filariasis and Japanese Encephalitis, not malaria or dengue, and reversing Anopheles and Aedes is the classic trap here. Question 12, safe to attempt, asks which disease the BCG vaccine protects against. The correct answer is tuberculosis, since BCG stands for Bacillus Calmette-Guerin, a live attenuated vaccine against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, given at birth, intra-dermally in the left arm. The trap to avoid is confusing it with OPV, which protects against polio, or DPT, which covers diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus, BCG equals TB is a direct one-to-one fact to remember. Question 13, safe to attempt, asks what characteristic symptom zinc deficiency in paddy produces. The correct answer is white bud, where new leaves turn pale or white, this being the most common micronutrient deficiency in South Karnataka paddy fields. The trap to avoid is confusing this with interveinal chlorosis, which is iron deficiency, or hollow heart, which is boron deficiency in groundnut, white bud specifically links to zinc. Question 14, marked safe to attempt, begins at the bottom of the page, its content continuing on the next page.
75: On this page we cover three important exam questions. First, DAP, or Di-ammonium Phosphate, contains 18 percent nitrogen and 46 percent P2O5, making it a double fertiliser widely used as a basal dose at planting. Do not confuse it with MOP, which contains potassium. Second, let us understand Pellagra, a deficiency disease caused by lack of Vitamin B3, also called Niacin. Its classic presentation is remembered by the four Ds, that is Dermatitis, Diarrhoea, Dementia, and eventually Death if untreated. Remember, Vitamin B1 deficiency causes Beriberi, not Pellagra, so B1 equals Beriberi, B3 equals Pellagra, and B12 equals Pernicious anaemia. Third, students, which plant cell structure carries out photosynthesis. The answer is the Chloroplast, the organelle containing chlorophyll and the enzyme systems for the light and dark reactions. Mitochondria, in contrast, are the site of respiration and energy release, not photosynthesis, and ribosomes synthesise proteins. Keep these three facts fresh: DAP composition, the four Ds of Pellagra, and chloroplast versus mitochondria function, since they are frequently tested together in general science sections.
76: Now, students, let us continue with general knowledge and science questions. Karnataka's Arogya Karnataka scheme is an extension of Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, the central health programme, and it extends coverage to families above the PM-JAY income threshold, making Karnataka's health insurance coverage broader than the central scheme alone. Do not confuse this with MGNREGS, which is a rural employment scheme, or Janani Suraksha Yojana, which is a maternal health cash incentive, not hospitalisation insurance. Next, regarding kala-azar, also known as visceral leishmaniasis, in Karnataka, the correct fact is that Karnataka has achieved kala-azar free status, with no endemic transmission in the state, a significant public health achievement. Remember that kala-azar is caused by Leishmania, a protozoan parasite, and is transmitted by the sandfly, not the Anopheles mosquito. These two facts, Arogya Karnataka as a PM-JAY extension and Karnataka's kala-azar free status, are important state health scheme points frequently tested in the exam.
77: Here, let us look at some biology and chemistry basics along with a calculation question. The photosynthesis equation produces glucose as its primary product, and the molecular formula of glucose is C6H12O6, the main energy currency of plant metabolism. Do not confuse this with C12H22O11, which is sucrose or table sugar, a disaccharide. Next comes an important calculation. If a farmer applies two bags of urea, each 50 kilograms, to a 1 acre field, how many kilograms of pure nitrogen does this supply. The total urea works out to 100 kilograms, and since urea contains 46 percent nitrogen, the nitrogen supplied equals 100 multiplied by 0.46, which is 46 kilograms of nitrogen. Many candidates mistakenly write 100 kilograms, forgetting that only 46 percent of urea is actual nitrogen. Remember the working formula, total urea in kilograms multiplied by 0.46 equals nitrogen supplied. Finally, which biofertiliser forms a symbiotic association with the roots of cereal crops to enhance nitrogen availability. The answer is Azospirillum, a free-living soil bacterium that associates with roots of rice, maize, wheat, and jowar, fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the rhizosphere, unlike Rhizobium which is exclusively a legume symbiont.
78: On this page we continue with disease classification and crop science. Which disease among tuberculosis, dengue, ringworm, and malaria is caused by a protozoan organism. The answer is Malaria, caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan parasite transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. Remember, tuberculosis is bacterial, dengue is viral, and ringworm, despite its name, is fungal and has nothing to do with worms, so malaria alone equals protozoan. Next, which crop is classified as a Short-Day Plant, or SDP. The answer is Jowar, or Sorghum, a classic Short-Day Plant requiring long nights to flower, and in Karnataka jowar flowers during October to November when nights are longer after the September equinox. Wheat, by contrast, is a Long-Day Plant, while tomato and cotton are Day-Neutral Plants that flower regardless of photoperiod. Finally, we begin a question on irrigation water quality, asking about the maximum safe Electrical Conductivity, or EC, for irrigation water that can be used on all crops without restriction, a topic we will complete on the next page.
79: Let us continue with irrigation water quality and soil science. The maximum safe Electrical Conductivity for irrigation water usable on all crops and soil types without restriction is 0.75 dS per metre, considered the low salinity hazard threshold. Above this level, salt-sensitive crops begin showing yield reduction, while 3.0 dS per metre is the harmful threshold affecting most crops. Next, what does a high Sodium Absorption Ratio, or SAR, value in irrigation water indicate. The answer is high sodium content relative to calcium and magnesium, known as the sodium hazard. High SAR means excess sodium, which disperses soil particles, reduces permeability, and creates a sodic, impermeable hardpan. Remember that EC measures total dissolved salts overall, not sodium specifically, and gypsum is the solution added to counter high-SAR water. Finally, under the WHO pesticide toxicity classification, a moderately hazardous pesticide carries a Yellow colour label on its packaging, with examples including chlorpyrifos and dichlorvos, commonly used in Karnataka's cotton, vegetable, and paddy crops.
80: Here we complete the pesticide classification topic and move to food safety and history. Remember the WHO colour code, Red equals Class 1a or 1b, extremely or highly hazardous, Yellow equals Class 2, moderately hazardous, Blue equals Class 3, slightly hazardous, and Green equals Class U, unlikely hazardous, which includes Bt spray and copper compounds. Next, what is the Pre-Harvest Interval, or PHI, and why is it important for food safety. PHI is the minimum number of days between the last pesticide spray and harvest, allowing the pesticide to break down to safe levels before the produce is consumed. Do not confuse this with the spray interval, which is the gap between successive sprays. Finally, students, when was Endosulfan completely banned in India. The answer is 2011, when the Supreme Court of India banned it completely, following evidence of neurological damage to children in Kasaragod district of Kerala, caused by aerial spraying on cashew plantations near the Karnataka border. Remember, Endosulfan is not merely restricted, it is fully banned in India since 2011.
81: Now, students, this page gives us a rapid revision table of ten high-yield facts, the kind you should read the night before the examination. Urea has 46 percent nitrogen, the highest of any solid fertiliser. DAP composition is 18 percent nitrogen plus 46 percent P2O5, called the double fertiliser. Karnataka's black soil pH ranges from 7.5 to 8.5, alkaline, where iron and zinc deficiency are common. Nano Urea, made by IFFCO, was launched in 2021 as a foliar spray, where 500 millilitres replaces one 45 kilogram urea bag. Caloric values are carbohydrates 4 kilocalories per gram, proteins 4 kilocalories per gram, and fats 9 kilocalories per gram. The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K, remembered by the acronym ADEK, stored in the body's fat. Ragi, or finger millet, has the highest calcium of any cereal grain, about 344 milligrams per 100 grams. For vectors, malaria is spread by the female Anopheles mosquito while dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti. Photoperiodism groups crops as Short-Day Plants like jowar, rice, and onion, Long-Day Plants like wheat and barley, and Day-Neutral Plants like tomato, cotton, and maize. Finally, pesticide label colours are Red for extremely hazardous, Yellow for Class 2, Blue for Class 3, and Green for safe.

84: Now, students, remember this key theme, history built this landscape, geography determines what grows, and an Agricultural Officer who understands both can do the job far better than one who merely memorised facts. Karnataka History and Geography is the highest-weightage unit in Paper 1, contributing 20 to 25 questions, and this edition adds three new sub-sections, Karnataka Soil Geography using ICAR classification, Karnataka's Agro-Climatic Zones under the 10-zone state classification, and Karnataka's Administrative Structure. Now begins Section 3.1, Ancient Karnataka, from the Kadambas to the Rashtrakutas. Karnataka's recorded political history begins in the 4th century CE with the Kadamba dynasty, the first to use Kannada as an official language in inscriptions.
85: Here we see the quick reference table of ancient Karnataka dynasties. The Kadambas ruled from 345 to 525 CE, capital Banavasi in Uttara Kannada, and were the first rulers to use Kannada in inscriptions, issuing land grants called agraharas to Brahmin settlements. The Western Gangas ruled 350 to 1000 CE from Talakad near Mysuru, known for tank irrigation, building hundreds of irrigation tanks across South Karnataka. The Badami Chalukyas ruled 543 to 757 CE from Vatapi, that is Badami in Bagalkot, and their ruler Pulakesi II defeated Harsha in 618 CE, building rock-cut temples at Badami, Aihole, and Pattadakal. The Rashtrakutas ruled 753 to 973 CE from Manyakheta, that is Malkhed in Kalaburagi, at their peak controlling most of India under Amoghavarsha I, their greatest ruler. The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani ruled 973 to 1198 CE from Kalyani in Bidar district, the period of Basavanna's Veerashaiva movement with extensive temple construction. For the exam, remember Kadambas as the first Karnataka dynasty founded in 345 CE at Banavasi, Rashtrakutas as a pan-Indian power, Badami Chalukyas famous for Pulakesi II's defeat of Harsha, and Western Chalukyas for Basavanna's era.
86: On this page, a did-you-know note tells us the Aihole inscription of 634 CE, found in Bagalkot district, is one of the earliest dated Sanskrit inscriptions in the Deccan, composed by court poet Ravikirti, recording Pulakesi II's victories including his defeat of Harsha of Kanauj. The Agri Lens notes that tank irrigation started by the Western Gangas laid the foundation of Karnataka's traditional water management, with thousands of tanks called keres built during the Ganga period, particularly in the Kaveri basin, still used for irrigation today. Now, students, Section 3.2 covers Medieval Karnataka, the Hoysalas and the Vijayanagara Empire, both directly relevant to land administration history. The Hoysala Dynasty ruled 1026 to 1343 CE from Dwarasamudra, present-day Halebidu in Hassan district, known for star-shaped temple architecture at Belur and Halebidu, and importantly for the exam, Hoysala inscriptions documented a sophisticated land revenue system classifying land by fertility, crop type, and irrigation status. The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty, with its capital at Hampi on the south bank of the Tungabhadra river, and its greatest ruler was Krishnadevaraya, 1509 to 1529 CE, who expanded the empire to its peak and authored the Telugu Veda.
87: Let us understand the Vijayanagara Empire's agricultural legacy, which included irrigation canals from the Tungabhadra river, classified crop land, and the introduction of sugarcane cultivation in the Deccan. Importantly, the land classification system of nanja for wet or irrigated land and gadu for dry or rainfed land originated in this period and is still used in Karnataka's RTC documents today, that is the Record of Rights, Tenancy and Crops. The field-relevance dialogue explains that nanja land receives canal water, tank water, or well irrigation, while gadu land depends entirely on rainfall, and this classification matters for schemes like PM Fasal Bima Yojana, since premium rates and coverage differ for irrigated and rainfed crops. Watch out, the Battle of Talikota in 1565 CE marks the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire, and this must not be confused with the Battle of Panipat. Talikota is located in present-day Vijayapura district of Karnataka, making it a frequently tested Karnataka geography-history crossover question. Remember the trick, Vijayanagara was founded in 1336, peaked under Krishnadevaraya from 1509 to 1529, and fell in 1565, these two dates covering 90 percent of Vijayanagara questions.
88: Now, students, Section 3.3 covers Modern Karnataka, the Mysore Wadiyars, Independence, and State Formation. Hyder Ali seized power in Mysore in 1761 CE, organising revenue and military reforms and introducing sericulture. Tipu Sultan ruled 1782 to 1799 CE, introducing large-scale sericulture, conducting a revenue survey, modernising irrigation, and falling at the Battle of Seringapatam in 1799. After Tipu's defeat, the British restored Wadiyar rule in 1799, and Mysore became a model princely state. Diwan M. Visvesvaraya served from 1912 to 1918, overseeing the KRS Dam project and industrial development, and his birthday, 15 September, is celebrated as National Engineers Day. The KRS Dam, that is Krishna Raja Sagara Dam on the Kaveri at Mandya, was constructed from 1911 to 1924 and was Visvesvaraya's masterpiece, the largest masonry dam in Asia when built. In 1947, Maharaja Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar signed the Instrument of Accession, merging Mysore with India. States Reorganisation followed the S.K. Fazl Ali Commission of 1953 to 55, and Mysore State was formed on 1 November 1956, later renamed Karnataka on 1 November 1973 under Chief Minister D. Devaraj Urs, who also brought the Land Reform Act of 1974.
89: Here the Agri Lens tells us that Tipu Sultan's introduction of sericulture on a commercial scale in the Mysore region during the 1790s is the most directly traceable historical root of Karnataka's modern silk industry, and today Karnataka produces over 70 percent of India's silk, with an AO in Ramanagara or Mysuru administering this 18th-century agricultural innovation even now. Now, students, Section 3.4 begins, Physical Geography, Karnataka's Five Physiographic Regions. Karnataka's physical geography is defined by five distinct regions, each with its own climate, soil, and crop profile, forming the foundation for understanding the state's agricultural diversity, and an AO's field posting will almost always fall within one of these zones. The North Karnataka Dry Zone covers Kalaburagi, Vijayapura, Bidar, Raichur, Yadgir, and Koppal, a flat Deccan plateau at 500 to 750 millimetres rainfall, with black cotton soil growing jowar, cotton, tur dal, chickpea, and sunflower. The North-East Transition Zone covers Vijayanagara, Chitradurga, and Davangere, with mixed red and black soil at 600 to 900 millimetres rainfall, growing paddy under TB command, cotton, maize, and groundnut. The Central Dry Zone covers Tumakuru, Hassan east, Kolar, Chikkaballapura, and Bengaluru Rural, with red laterite and red sandy loam soil growing ragi, groundnut, mulberry, and vegetables.
90: Let us complete the physiographic regions table. The Malnad, or Highland Zone covers Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru, Shivamogga west, and Hassan west, at 600 to 1900 metre altitude with 1500 to 3000 millimetres rainfall, laterite and red clay soil, growing coffee, cardamom, pepper, arecanut, and paddy. The Coastal Zone covers Dakshina Kannada and Uttara Kannada, receiving up to 4000 millimetres rainfall on coastal laterite and alluvial soil, growing paddy, coconut, arecanut, banana, and cashew. Remember, the Western Ghats lie in the west while the dryland plateau lies in the east, and rainfall decreases dramatically moving east of the Ghats, from 4000 millimetres on the coast to just 500 millimetres in the north-east, a rain-shadow effect explaining why North Karnataka is drought-prone. Did you know, Karnataka's Western Ghats were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, covering approximately 5500 square kilometres of evergreen and semi-evergreen forest, among the world's eight hottest biodiversity hotspots. Now, students, Section 3.5 begins, Rivers, Dams, and Irrigation Command Areas, covering the four major river basins, Kaveri, Tungabhadra-Krishna, Sharavathi-west flowing rivers, and the Godavari.
91: Here is the continuing table of Karnataka's rivers, dams, and command areas. The Kaveri river's KRS Dam, that is Krishna Raja Sagara, is located in Mandya district, commanding 1.24 lakh hectares of paddy and sugarcane, built in 1924 by Visvesvaraya, and Mandya is known as the sugar bowl. The Hemavathi river, a Kaveri tributary, has the Hemavathi Dam in Hassan district, commanding 1.64 lakh hectares of paddy, ragi, and groundnut, serving as Hassan's main irrigation source and also feeding Tumakuru. The Tungabhadra river's TB Dam, part of the Tungabhadra Project, is located at Hospete in Vijayanagara district, commanding 3.62 lakh hectares of paddy, cotton, and maize, built in 1953, with the TB Board headquartered at Hospete. The Krishna river's Almatti Dam, part of the Upper Krishna Project, is in Vijayapura district, commanding 6.12 lakh hectares, the largest command area in Karnataka, growing cotton, jowar, and paddy, and built in 2013. The Ghataprabha river's Hidkal Dam in Belagavi district commands 1.56 lakh hectares of sugarcane and paddy, supporting North Karnataka's sugarcane irrigation.

The crop grown in any district is determined by its soil type, rainfall, temperature, and irrigation access, following the physiographic zonation already described. The North Karnataka Dry Zone, with black cotton soil at 500 to 700 millimetres rainfall, is Karnataka's pulses belt, the largest tur dal producing region, with Almatti and TB command adding irrigated paddy.
