154: Now, students, we begin the Practice Questions section, working through 33 questions, each with a strategy note, the correct answer, the reasoning, and a common trap to avoid. Question 1 asks which part of the Indian Constitution contains the Fundamental Rights. The correct answer is Part 3, Articles 12 to 35, which are justiciable and enforceable through courts, including the Supreme Court under Article 32. The trap to avoid is confusing this with Part 4, which contains the Directive Principles, a frequent mix-up, while Part 2 covers citizenship and Part 9, added by the 73rd Amendment, covers Panchayati Raj. Question 2 asks which Constitutional Amendment removed the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights, and to which Article it was moved. The correct answer is the 44th Amendment of 1978, moving it to Article 300A. The reasoning explains the 44th Amendment removed the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights, where it was Article 31, and placed it in Part 12 as Article 300A instead. The trap to avoid is confusing this with the 42nd Amendment of 1976, which made major changes but did not touch the Right to Property; that change specifically belongs to the 44th Amendment, not Article 31.
155: On this page we continue our practice questions on the Constitution. First, we look at Article 48, which is a Directive Principle of State Policy directing the state to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines. It also mentions prohibiting the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle, and it sits in Part 4, the DPSPs. Do not confuse it with Article 45, which is about free compulsory education, now superseded by Article 21A after the 86th Amendment, Article 48A, which is about environmental protection, or Article 43, which deals with a living wage for workers. Next, let us understand the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992. This amendment inserted Part 9, covering Articles 243 to 243-O, dealing with Panchayats, and added the Eleventh Schedule, which lists 29 subjects that may be transferred to Panchayats. It came into force on 24 April 1993. Remember, Part 9-A and the Twelfth Schedule belong to the 74th Amendment, which covers Urban Local Bodies or Municipalities, not rural Panchayats. So the simple rule is, 73rd equals Part 9 plus Eleventh Schedule equals rural, while 74th equals Part 9-A plus Twelfth Schedule equals urban.
156: Now, students, let us understand where agriculture sits in our Constitution. Agriculture is Entry 14 of the State List, which is List 2 in the Seventh Schedule. This means state governments hold primary legislative authority over agriculture, and states can enact agricultural laws, such as Karnataka's APMC Act and Land Reform Act, without needing central approval. Do not confuse this with the Concurrent List, which includes forests under Entry 17A and food distribution under Entry 33, both of which involve both the Centre and the states. Agriculture itself, under Entry 14, is exclusively on the State List. The Sixth Schedule, by contrast, covers tribal areas, and the Ninth Schedule protects land reform laws from judicial review. Next, let us look at the Eleventh Schedule, which was added by the 73rd Amendment. It lists 29 subjects that state legislatures may optionally transfer to Panchayats. These subjects include agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, and poverty alleviation, among others. Remember, 18 is the number of subjects in the Twelfth Schedule, which is for Urban Local Bodies under the 74th Amendment, so do not mix up these two numbers, 29 for Panchayats and 18 for Municipalities, since this pairing is a very standard trap question in the exam.
157: Here, we look at land reform legislation in Karnataka. The Karnataka Land Reform Act was originally enacted in 1961, but the 1974 amendment, brought in under Chief Minister D. Devaraj Urs, is the most significant one. It imposed land ceilings, abolished tenancy rights of large landholders, and gave tenant farmers who had cultivated land for 12 or more years ownership rights over that land. So when a question asks about land reform actually happening in Karnataka, the answer points to 1974, not 1961. Let us also understand a very famous constitutional fact. Dr B R Ambedkar described Article 32, the Right to Constitutional Remedies, as the heart and soul of the Constitution. This article allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court directly to enforce any Fundamental Right, and without it, other rights would be hollow. Today, Article 21, the Right to Life, is often called the most important article because of judicial expansions, but Ambedkar's specific statement about heart and soul refers to Article 32. This is a direct recall question, so remember, the answer is Article 32.
158: On this page we study the 97th Constitutional Amendment of 2011. This amendment gave constitutional status to cooperative societies. It did this by adding Article 43B as a Directive Principle of State Policy and by including cooperative societies in Article 19(1)(c) as a fundamental right. This strengthens the legal standing of PACS, that is Primary Agricultural Credit Societies, and Karnataka's milk cooperatives under KMF. Do not confuse this with Gram Panchayats, which were given constitutional recognition by the 73rd Amendment in 1992, or agricultural universities, which fall under state legislation. This 97th Amendment specifically targets cooperatives, an important and often underestimated piece of constitutional law for agricultural officers. Next, let us understand Article 48A, which directs the state to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. It was added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976 and provides the constitutional basis for environmental protection legislation. Remember, Article 51A(g) is the citizens' Fundamental Duty to protect the environment, not a state directive, so the rule is, Article 48A is the state's environmental duty, and Article 51A(g) is the citizen's environmental duty. Both were added by the same 42nd Amendment of 1976.
159: Let us understand the Karnataka APMC Act of 1966, which was amended in 2020. This 2020 amendment allowed farmers to sell their agricultural produce outside the regulated APMC yard, directly to private buyers, at the farm gate, or on online platforms, without paying the standard market cess. This increased farmer choice in marketing. The amendment did not allow establishing new APMCs or make any changes to import duty, so the key change to remember is, outside the APMC yard, no cess. This 2020 amendment was Karnataka's parallel to the central Farm Laws, which were later repealed. Now, students, let us look at the Gram Sabha, which is mentioned in Article 243A. The Gram Sabha is defined as the body consisting of all persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village comprised within the area of a Panchayat at the village level. In simpler terms, it is the assembly of all voters in the village. Do not confuse this with the Gram Panchayat, which is the elected governing body, having a President and elected ward members. The distinction tested often is, Gram Sabha equals all voters, while Gram Panchayat equals the elected body only.
160: On this page we study the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution. It was created by the 1st Constitutional Amendment of 1951 to protect land reform laws from being challenged for violating Fundamental Rights. This amendment inserted Articles 31A and 31B, and laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are protected from judicial challenge on grounds of violating Fundamental Rights. Zamindari abolition laws and the Karnataka Land Reform Act were placed here. The original Constitution of 1950 did not have the Ninth Schedule, it was added specifically because early land reform laws were being struck down by courts for violating the Right to Property. Next, let us understand Article 300A, which states that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. This is the current provision for the Right to Property, after it was moved from the Fundamental Rights list by the 44th Amendment of 1978. Before that, Article 19(1)(f) was the original Fundamental Right to property, and the earlier Article 31 has now been deleted, with the provision moved to Article 300A in Part 12 of the Constitution.
161: Let us understand the 42nd Constitutional Amendment of 1976, which transferred education from the State List to the Concurrent List. Now, both the Central and State governments can legislate on education, and this is the constitutional basis under which the Right to Education Act of 2009 was enacted as a central law. Remember, agriculture remains firmly in the State List under Entry 14, this is an important stable fact. Forests, under Entry 17A, and some other subjects, were already in the Concurrent List or were also shifted by the 42nd Amendment. So education is the most standard answer whenever a question asks what the 42nd Amendment transferred to the Concurrent List. Now, students, let us understand tenancy reform. Under the Karnataka Land Reform Act of 1961, and its 1974 amendment, tenant farmers who had cultivated land for 12 or more years before 1974 gained the right to ownership of that land. The original 1961 Act laid the framework, but the transformative provision was the 1974 amendment. This was the land to the tiller reform under Chief Minister D. Devaraj Urs, so remember this pairing well, since the APMC Act and the Cooperative Act are entirely different pieces of legislation.
162: On this page we study the Twelfth Schedule of the Constitution, which lists 18 subjects for Municipalities, that is, Urban Local Bodies. This Twelfth Schedule was added by the 74th Amendment of 1992. This is the urban counterpart to the Eleventh Schedule, which lists 29 subjects for Panchayats under the 73rd Amendment. Remember this pairing, 29 subjects for rural Panchayats and 18 subjects for urban Municipalities. Next, let us understand a Fundamental Right relevant to farmers. Article 19(1)(g) guarantees every citizen the right to carry on any trade, profession, or business. This is the Fundamental Right basis for challenging any mandatory rule that would force farmers to sell only through the APMC yard. A farmer's right to choose their marketing channel flows from this article. Do not confuse it with Article 19(1)(a), which is freedom of speech and expression, or Article 19(1)(c), which is the right to form associations, relevant for forming cooperatives. So remember, Article 19(1)(g) equals trade and profession, which is the commercial freedom underlying agricultural marketing liberty.
163: Here, we revise the Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution, which is relevant to Panchayats. It lists 29 subjects that state legislatures may optionally transfer to Panchayats. These include agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, rural housing, education, health, and poverty alleviation, among others. Remember, 18 is the number for the Twelfth Schedule, which covers Urban Local Bodies, while 29 is for the Eleventh Schedule, for Panchayats. These two numbers are commonly mixed up in the exam, so keep them clear. Now, let us understand the Karnataka Souharda Cooperative Act, which was enacted in 1997. The Souharda model is a more democratic form of cooperative society, with equal voting rights regardless of share capital. Karnataka's Souharda cooperatives include credit, dairy, and agricultural marketing cooperatives. Next, we look at Article 243G, which gives Panchayats powers and functions that state legislatures may devolve. Among the options, banking and insurance services is NOT listed as a subject in the Eleventh Schedule, since banking and insurance is a Union List subject, Entry 45, and cannot be devolved to Panchayats.
164: On this page we continue with banking and insurance, confirming it is a Union List subject that cannot be devolved to Panchayats through the Eleventh Schedule, while agriculture, minor irrigation, and poverty alleviation are all genuine Eleventh Schedule Panchayat subjects. Now, let us understand the 42nd Constitutional Amendment of 1976, sometimes called the mini-Constitution. This amendment added Fundamental Duties under Article 51A, added Article 48A for environmental protection, and added the words socialist and secular to the Preamble. It did NOT move the Right to Property out of Fundamental Rights, that change was made later by the 44th Amendment of 1978, after Indira Gandhi's government fell. This is a very common trap, so remember, the property right change happened under the 44th Amendment, not the 42nd. Next, we study the Karnataka Zilla Panchayat, which operates under the Karnataka Zilla Panchayats Act of 1983, amended after 1993 to conform with the 73rd Amendment. The Zilla Panchayat sits at the district tier, the top tier, of Karnataka's three-tier Panchayati Raj structure.
165: Here, we confirm that the Zilla Panchayat in Karnataka sits at the district level, the top tier of the three-tier structure of Gram Panchayat, Taluk Panchayat, and Zilla Panchayat. It operates under the Karnataka Zilla Panchayats, Taluk Panchayat Samithis, Mandal Panchayats and Nyaya Panchayats Act of 1983, as amended after the 73rd Amendment. Remember, the Agricultural Officer reports to the Zilla Panchayat Agriculture Standing Committee. Now, let us understand what non-justiciable means for Directive Principles of State Policy. It means DPSPs cannot be directly enforced by any court if the government fails to implement them. Neither the Supreme Court nor the High Courts can enforce DPSPs directly, DPSPs apply to the state's obligations, not citizens' rights, and DPSPs do not override Fundamental Rights categorically, though the 42nd Amendment did give them precedence in some situations. So remember, DPSPs are moral and political obligations on the state, not legally enforceable rights.
166: On this page we study the effect of placing the Karnataka Land Reform Act's land ceiling laws in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution. Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are protected from judicial challenge on grounds of violating Fundamental Rights. The 1st Amendment of 1951 created the Ninth Schedule specifically to shield land reform laws from being struck down by courts under the Right to Property. Remember, the Ninth Schedule is NOT a time limited protection, it does NOT require Supreme Court approval for amendments, this protection is designed to let Parliament implement radical land reforms without judicial obstruction. Now, students, let us understand Article 356, President's Rule. Parliament must approve the proclamation within 2 months by a simple majority, and it can be continued for a maximum of 3 years, though extension beyond 1 year requires both a National Emergency to be in force AND the Election Commission to certify that elections cannot be held. Do not confuse the 30 day figure, that is the RTI response deadline, a completely different law. Remember, President's Rule parliamentary approval equals 2 months, and maximum duration equals 3 years with special conditions.
167: Let us understand Article 352, the National Emergency provision, which requires a special majority for Parliamentary approval, that is two-thirds of members present and voting in each House, provided they also form a majority of the total membership of that House. This is a higher threshold than the ordinary two-thirds majority used for constitutional amendments. Remember, Article 356, President's Rule, needs only a simple majority, much easier, while Article 352, National Emergency, needs this special double filter majority. Confusing the majority requirements of 352 and 356 is a standard trap. Now, here is an important date for administrators. The Right to Information Act 2005 came into force on 12 October 2005, and the prescribed application fee is Rs 10. BPL card holders are exempt from payment. Additional charges apply for providing documents, Rs 2 per page for photocopies. Do not confuse this with Independence Day, 15 August, or Republic Day, 26 January, which are common wrong guesses because they are memorable national dates. Both the RTI date and the fee amount are individually tested facts.
168: On this page, we look at a practical RTI scenario. If a farmer files an RTI application with the Taluk Agriculture Office and does not receive a response within 30 days, the First Appeal goes to a senior officer within the same public authority, within 30 days of the missed deadline or of receiving an unsatisfactory response. The Second Appeal goes to the State Information Commission, which in Karnataka is the Karnataka State Information Commission, or KSIC. Remember, High Courts and the Supreme Court are not the appellate bodies under RTI, that is a separate writ jurisdiction matter, different from the RTI appeal mechanism. The Central Information Commission, or CIC, handles second appeals for central government authorities, while KSIC handles Karnataka state authority appeals. Now, students, let us look at a Consumer Protection Act scenario. A farmer files a complaint against a pesticide company for selling an ineffective product, and the claim is worth Rs 75 lakh. We need to determine which Consumer Commission has jurisdiction over this claim amount.
169: Here, under the Consumer Protection Act of 2019, we learn the answer to our scenario. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, or DCDRC, handles complaints up to Rs 1 crore. Since the Rs 75 lakh claim is below Rs 1 crore, it falls under the District Commission's jurisdiction. Remember, the State Commission handles claims from Rs 1 crore to Rs 10 crore, and the National Commission handles claims above Rs 10 crore. The APMC has no jurisdiction over product liability claims against input manufacturers. Now, let us understand IFFCO, the Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative. It was established in 1967 and is registered as a Multi-State Cooperative Society, currently under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act of 2002. IFFCO has approximately 36,000 member cooperative societies across India and operates major fertiliser plants at Kandla, Kalol, Phulpur, Aonla, and Paradeep. Remember, IFFCO is NOT a private company, it is not under the Companies Act, and it is not a state cooperative since its membership crosses state boundaries. So the key fact is, IFFCO equals 1967, and it is a Multi-State Cooperative.
170: On this page we study the National Dairy Development Board, or NDDB. It was established in 1965, and is headquartered at Anand, Gujarat. Dr Verghese Kurien, called the Father of the White Revolution, was its founding architect and served as chairman from 1965 to 1998. NDDB implemented Operation Flood, from 1970 to 1996, which made India the world's largest milk producer. Remember, M S Swaminathan is associated with the Green Revolution, that is food grains, not the White Revolution, which is dairy. So remember, 1965 equals NDDB's founding, and 1970 equals the launch of Operation Flood. Now, students, let us understand the Karnataka Milk Federation, or KMF. It markets all its dairy products under the Nandini brand, including milk, curd, butter, ghee, ice cream, and cheese. KMF is the second largest dairy cooperative federation in India by milk procurement, after GCMMF, the Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation, which markets the AMUL brand. Remember, Vijaya is the brand of the Andhra Pradesh dairy cooperative, a different state, while Aavin is Tamil Nadu, and Milma is Kerala, and Mother Dairy is a separate central government cooperative structure.
171: Now, students, this page begins our Rapid Revision section, with 12 high yield facts to read the night before the examination. These cover the highest frequency testable points from this unit, under the Karnataka AO AAO Paper 1 format. Fact one, Fundamental Rights are in Articles 12 to 35, Part 3, and are justiciable, enforceable in courts. Fact two, DPSPs are in Articles 36 to 51, Part 4, and are non-justiciable, a moral and political obligation on the state. Fact three, the Right to Property is Article 300A, a constitutional right, not a Fundamental Right, moved from Article 31 by the 44th Amendment of 1978. Fact four, Article 48 covers agriculture and animal husbandry, a DPSP, while Article 48A covers environmental protection, added by the 42nd Amendment of 1976. Fact five, the 73rd Amendment of 1992 covers Part 9, the Article 243 series, Panchayati Raj, and the Eleventh Schedule, in force from 24 April 1993. Fact six, the Eleventh Schedule has 29 Panchayat subjects under the 73rd Amendment, while the Twelfth Schedule has 18 Municipality subjects under the 74th Amendment, rural versus urban. Fact seven, agriculture is in the Seventh Schedule State List, Entry 14, giving state governments primary legislative authority over agriculture.
172: Let us continue our Rapid Revision. Fact eight, Emergency Provisions, Article 352, National Emergency, needs two-thirds majority, Article 356, President's Rule, needs a simple majority and a maximum of 3 years, and Article 360, Financial Emergency, has never been proclaimed. Fact nine, the RTI Act 2005 came into force on 12 October 2005, with a Rs 10 fee, a 30 day response window, and KSIC as the second appeal authority in Karnataka. Fact ten, under the Consumer Protection Act 2019, the District Commission handles claims up to Rs 1 crore, the State Commission Rs 1 to 10 crore, the National Commission above Rs 10 crore, and a farmer is treated as a consumer for input purchases. Fact eleven, NDDB was established in 1965 by Dr Verghese Kurien at Anand, and Operation Flood ran from 1970 to 1996, making India the world's largest milk producer. Fact twelve, KMF, the Karnataka Milk Federation, uses the Anand Pattern, with the Nandini brand, 13 District Milk Unions, and 2.6 million members, the second largest dairy cooperative in India. After this, the page lists References and Further Reading, beginning with Constitutional Texts, the Constitution of India from the Ministry of Law and Justice, the 73rd Amendment Act 1992 from the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, and the 97th Amendment Act 2011 from the Ministry of Cooperation, followed by Central Legislation, the RTI Act 2005, the Consumer Protection Act 2019, and the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act 2002.
173: This page continues the References and Further Reading section. Under Karnataka State Legislation, it lists the Karnataka Land Reform Act 1961, with its 1974 and 2020 amendments, referencing karnataka.gov.in and the Bhoomi portal, the Karnataka APMC Act 1966 with its 2020 amendment, from the Karnataka State Agriculture Marketing Department, the Karnataka Souharda Cooperative Act 1997, from the Karnataka Cooperative Department, and the Karnataka Zilla Panchayats Act 1983, as amended, from Karnataka Rural Development and Panchayat Raj. Under Dairy and Cooperative References, it lists the National Dairy Development Board, referencing nddb.coop for the history of Operation Flood and the Anand Pattern, the Karnataka Milk Federation, referencing kmfnandini.com for the Nandini brand and district union list, and IFFCO, referencing iffco.in for multi-state cooperative registration details. Under Standard Reference Books, it lists M Laxmikanth's Indian Polity as the most widely used reference for PSC polity preparation, D D Basu's Introduction to the Constitution of India for deeper constitutional provisions, and Karnataka PSC Previous Year Papers from kpsc.kar.gov.in. Finally, a note reminds candidates that constitutional provisions cited in this chapter are accurate as of the knowledge cutoff date, and that for any constitutional amendment passed after June 2025, candidates should check the official Ministry of Law and Justice website before the examination.
174: On this page we begin Unit 5, Rural Development and Schemes, covering Central Schemes, Karnataka Schemes, the MSP Mechanism, FPOs, PMKSY, Jal Jeevan Mission, Social Security, and Credit and Insurance. This is Unit 5 of 8, carrying an estimated 22 to 28 questions, the highest weightage unit with the highest direct job relevance. The exam strategy notes that central schemes such as PM-Kisan, PMFBY, MGNREGS, and RKVY are safe topics, since amounts, launch years, and implementing agencies are frequently tested, while MSP and cost concepts are riskier. FPOs, PMKSY, Jal Jeevan Mission, and social security schemes are safe, easy marks, and Karnataka state schemes are moderately safe. For last night revision, re-read Section 6, focusing on PM-Kisan, which gives Rs 6,000 in 3 instalments, PMFBY from 2016, MGNREGS with its 100 days guarantee, the Soil Health Card with 14 parameters, PMKSY's 4 components, MSP cost concepts of A2 versus C2, Jal Jeevan Mission targets, and PMJJBY and PMSBY premium amounts. On field relevance, this unit IS the job description, since an Agricultural Officer spends 60 to 70 percent of working time implementing, explaining, verifying, and reporting on these schemes. The Unit Overview then opens with a scenario, it is the first week of December, and an Agricultural Officer at the Raitha Samparka Kendra in a North Karnataka taluk is managing a queue of 40 farmers, all waiting to check whether their PM-Kisan instalment for the December to March period has been credited to their accounts.
175: On this page, we meet a day in the life of an Agricultural Officer handling PM-Kisan cases and Farmer Producer Organisation queries, which introduces Unit 5 of the AO or AAO textbook. Unit 5 covers the landscape of central and Karnataka state government schemes for rural development and agriculture, organised into eight parts. These are central agricultural schemes like PM-Kisan and PMFBY, other central schemes such as RKVY, Soil Health Card, eNAM, and MGNREGS, Karnataka state-level programmes, agricultural credit and insurance, Farmer Producer Organisations or FPOs, the Minimum Support Price mechanism and price policy, PMKSY and Jal Jeevan Mission, and farmer social security schemes. Together, these programmes direct thousands of crores of rupees annually to farming households in Karnataka. Students, this unit is tested intensively in the examination, with 22 to 28 questions from this unit typical in Paper 1. The pattern focuses on scheme names and their full forms, year of launch, annual benefit amount or coverage, implementing agency, and Karnataka-specific data. The Agri Lens box lists the Agricultural Officer's five standard tasks in scheme implementation, starting with creating and verifying beneficiary lists using land records and Bhoomi or PM-Kisan portals, and conducting awareness camps at Gram Sabhas.
176: Now, students, let us look at the AO's five standard tasks continued from the previous page: coordinating with banks for Kisan Credit Card and insurance premium deduction, verifying crop loss for PMFBY claims, and submitting utilisation certificates for RKVY and state scheme funds. FPO promotion and MSP procurement facilitation are newer additions to this list. Moving to Core Concepts, section 5.1 covers PM-Kisan, the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi. This is the central government's flagship direct income support scheme for farmers. It was launched on 24 February 2019, with the first instalment backdated to December 2018. It provides 6,000 rupees per year to eligible farm families across India, paid in three equal instalments of 2,000 rupees each, covering April to July, August to November, and December to March. Eligibility is limited to landholder farmer families with cultivable land, where the name must appear in land records. The mode of transfer is Direct Benefit Transfer to an Aadhaar-linked bank account. Exclusions include income tax payers, constitutional post holders, government employees, and professionals such as doctors, lawyers, engineers, and chartered accountants. The implementing agency is the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare, with state governments maintaining beneficiary lists.
177: Here, we learn that Karnataka has over 50 lakh farmer families registered under PM-Kisan, as of 2024. The Agricultural Officer's specific role in this scheme is beneficiary list management. Farmers are added or removed based on land record updates from the Bhoomi portal, Karnataka's land records system. When a farmer buys land, sells land, or inherits land, the PM-Kisan status must be updated, and the AO coordinates with the Revenue Department at the Taluk office to ensure the Bhoomi portal and PM-Kisan portal records are consistent. A field example shows the AO resolving a farmer's grievance about a missing December instalment, explaining three common reasons: the bank account may not be Aadhaar-linked or KYC may be incomplete, the land record name in Bhoomi may not exactly match the PM-Kisan database, or the family may have been flagged in an eligibility verification. The AO advises checking beneficiary status on the pmkisan.gov.in portal. Here's the trick to remember: 6,000 rupees per year equals 3 times 2,000 rupees. The launch date to remember is December 2018 for the first instalment, and 24 February 2019 for the official launch ceremony. Both dates are frequently tested.
178: Let us understand section 5.2, the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, or PMFBY. This is India's comprehensive crop insurance scheme, launched on 18 February 2016, replacing the earlier National Agricultural Insurance Scheme and the Modified National Agricultural Insurance Scheme. It covers all food and oilseed crops, and annual commercial or horticultural crops for which past yield data is available. The premium rates paid by farmers are notably low: kharif crops at 2 percent of sum insured, rabi crops at 1.5 percent, and annual commercial or horticultural crops at 5 percent. The remaining premium balance is shared equally between the Centre and State after the farmer's share is deducted. Coverage spans pre-sowing, standing crop, post-harvest, and prevented sowing or planting risks. Claims are triggered using yield data from Crop Cutting Experiments, with the unit of insurance being the village or Gram Panchayat level. The implementing agency is the Ministry of Agriculture, working through empanelled insurance companies. In Karnataka, Raitha Siri is the state's PMFBY top-up scheme, and drone-based Crop Cutting Experiments are used for accurate yield estimation. When a crop failure is reported due to drought, flood, pest, or disease, the AO organises Crop Cutting Experiments at randomly selected survey numbers.
179: On this page, we learn that if actual yield falls below the threshold at a Crop Cutting Experiment location, all insured farmers in that unit automatically receive a proportional claim payment without needing to file individual loss reports. Watch out for a classic trap question: PMFBY and the Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme, known as RWBCIS, are two different schemes. PMFBY uses yield data from Crop Cutting Experiments to trigger claims, while RWBCIS uses weather data such as rainfall, temperature, and humidity from Automatic Weather Stations. Remember the premium memory trick: 2, 1.5, 5 , kharif is 2 percent, rabi is 1.5 percent, and commercial or horticultural crops are 5 percent, with government subsidising the bulk of the actuarial premium. Now, students, section 5.3 introduces other central agricultural schemes: RKVY, Soil Health Card, eNAM, MGNREGS, and the National Horticulture Mission. The Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, or RKVY, was launched in 2007 and revamped in 2019 as RKVY-RAFTAAR. It provides flexible funding for agriculture infrastructure, market development, and extension, with states preparing district action plans. In Karnataka, RKVY funds farm mechanisation, FPO promotion, and post-harvest infrastructure, and the AO submits district plans.
180: Let us continue with more central schemes in this table. The Soil Health Card Scheme, launched in 2015, tests every farmer's land every 2 years for 14 soil parameters including nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, pH, and electrical conductivity, with results provided in a card carrying fertiliser recommendations. The AO organises sample collection, coordinates with soil testing labs, and distributes the cards. Next, eNAM, the National Agriculture Market, launched in 2016, is an electronic trading platform linking over 1,000 APMCs across India, giving farmers price discovery across markets. In Karnataka, farmers in the Kolar tomato belt use eNAM for inter-state price discovery. PM Kisan Maan Dhan Yojana, launched in 2019, is a voluntary pension scheme for small and marginal farmers aged 18 to 40, providing 3,000 rupees per month pension at age 60, with a monthly contribution of 55 to 200 rupees. The National Food Security Mission, from 2007, focuses on increasing production of rice, wheat, pulses, coarse cereals, and oilseeds. The National Horticulture Mission, now called MIDH, from 2005, subsidises horticulture development including orchards and protected cultivation. And MGNREGS, the rural employment guarantee scheme, from 2005 as an Act and 2006 as implementation, guarantees 100 days of employment per household per year.
181: Continuing on MGNREGS, this scheme creates permanent assets while ensuring minimum wage, and the AO works with it for water conservation and land levelling, converging it with agriculture. Also on this page, PMGSY, the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, from the year 2000, provides all-weather road connectivity to habitations, improving farmers' ability to sell produce at distant APMCs and reducing spoilage during transport. Now, let us understand the Soil Health Card in detail. Samples are collected from every field, one sample per 2 hectares of irrigated land and one per 10 hectares of rainfed land, every two years. Each sample is tested for 12 parameters, made 14 in practice when including electrical conductivity and pH. The card is issued in Kannada in Karnataka. The Agri Lens box explains that this scheme reduces fertiliser misuse, particularly in North Karnataka's cotton belt where excess urea use has caused soil acidification. Here's the trick for scheme years: PMGSY equals 2000, National Horticulture Mission equals 2005, MGNREGS Act equals 2005, RKVY equals 2007, National Food Security Mission equals 2007, eNAM equals 2016, PMFBY equals 2016, Soil Health Card equals 2015, and PM-Kisan equals 2018 or 2019.
182: On this page, section 5.4 introduces Karnataka State Schemes for Agriculture. Karnataka operates a large portfolio of state-level agricultural schemes alongside central schemes, funded from the state budget, addressing Karnataka-specific priorities, and implemented by the Department of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare. Raitha Siri is a top-up to PMFBY, providing additional crop insurance compensation, and the AO coordinates PMFBY enrolment while verifying Raitha Siri eligibility alongside the PMFBY claim. Krishi Bhagya focuses on water conservation and drip irrigation for dryland farmers in rainfed areas, providing subsidy for farm pond construction, micro-irrigation, and pump sets for farmers with less than 2 hectares of dryland. The AO identifies eligible dryland farmers, supervises farm pond construction, and certifies completion for subsidy release. Raitha Samparka Kendra, or RSK, is a single-window service centre at the hobli or taluk level, offering seeds, fertilisers, scheme registration, soil testing, credit, and extension services, all managed by the AO. Pashu Bhagya provides livestock insurance for dairy and draught animals, with premium subsidy for cattle, buffalo, sheep, and goat, up to 50,000 rupees coverage per animal.
183: Continuing the Karnataka schemes table, Pashu Bhagya benefits livestock-owning farm families. Bhoo Chethana promotes soil and water conservation through an integrated watershed approach, involving watershed treatment, contour bunding, check dams, and vegetative barriers in degraded lands, and the AO supervises watershed works and certifies completed works. Karnataka Raitha Suraksha provides state compensation for crop loss not covered by PMFBY, based on input subsidy or crop loss assessment after a natural calamity, and the AO conducts Hani survey or girdavari and submits reports to the taluk office. A Did You Know box tells us that Krishi Bhagya specifically targets dryland farmers, since Karnataka has approximately 67 percent of its cultivated area under rainfed conditions, one of the highest rainfed percentages among major agricultural states. The farm pond programme under Krishi Bhagya has created thousands of small reservoirs across North Karnataka, enabling a second crop in years with bimodal rainfall. Now, section 5.5 begins, covering Agricultural Credit through the Kisan Credit Card, NABARD, and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies, or PACS.
184: Let us understand agricultural credit, the lifeline of farm investment. An Agricultural Officer routinely helps farmers navigate the credit system, from Kisan Credit Cards for crop loans to NABARD-refinanced term loans for farm equipment. Multiple institutions are involved: commercial banks, cooperative banks, regional rural banks, and the apex institution, NABARD. The Kisan Credit Card, or KCC, provides short-term revolving credit for crop production, covering input costs and post-harvest expenses, with an interest subvention of 2 percent on timely repayment. In Karnataka, farmers access KCC through Canara Bank, State Bank of India, and DCCB, with the AO helping farmers open KCC accounts at the Raitha Samparka Kendra. NABARD is the apex institution for agricultural credit, refinancing banks and regional rural banks, and funding watershed and rural infrastructure. Primary Agricultural Credit Societies, or PACS, are village-level cooperative societies providing short-term credit for seeds, fertilisers, and pesticides, connected to the District Cooperative Central Bank, or DCCB. Karnataka has over 5,000 PACS. The DCCB is the district-level apex of cooperative credit, refinanced by SCARDB and NABARD, with 31 DCCBs in Karnataka, one per district.
185: On this page, we learn the Kisan Credit Card scheme was launched in 1998 to 99 by NABARD, and has become the standard vehicle for agricultural crop loans. Farmers can withdraw up to their credit limit during the crop season, repay after harvest, and re-borrow for the next season. The interest subvention scheme makes KCC loans effectively at 4 percent per annum for prompt repayors. Remember, NABARD was established on 12 July 1982 on the recommendations of the Shivaraman Committee, with headquarters in Mumbai. The credit structure is three-tier: PACS at village level for crop loans, DCCB at district level refinancing PACS, and NABARD as the apex institution refinancing all banks. Now, section 5.6 begins, covering Farmer Producer Organisations, or FPOs, for collective marketing and value addition. An FPO is a collective of farmers, typically registered as a Producer Company under the Companies Act 2013 or as a cooperative, enabling small and marginal farmers to aggregate produce, access inputs collectively, and sell at better prices by eliminating intermediaries. The minimum membership to register is 10 farmer members under the Companies Act, though practical viability requires 300 to 500 members for commodity trading.
186: Continuing on FPOs, the central scheme for Formation and Promotion of 10,000 FPOs was launched in 2020 as a Central Sector Scheme under the Ministry of Agriculture, targeting 10,000 new FPOs in 5 years, by 2025, with priority given to small and marginal farmers, women farmers, and tribal farmers. Implementing agencies are SFAC, the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium, NABARD, and state cooperative departments. Financial support amounts to 18 lakh rupees per FPO over 3 years as grant, plus equity grant and credit guarantee. In Karnataka, FPOs have been promoted in tomato in Kolar district, pomegranate in Gadag district, and ragi and jowar belts. The AO's role is identifying potential FPO clusters, facilitating registration, and connecting FPOs with SFAC, NABARD, and buyers. An FPO aggregates produce from its member farmers and sells collectively, either to processors, exporters, retail chains, or government procurement agencies, giving bargaining power that individual small farmers lack. FPOs also bulk-purchase inputs at lower prices, provide custom hiring of machinery, and sometimes operate their own processing units. The three stages of FPO development are formation, stabilisation, and independence, when the FPO becomes financially self-sustaining.
187: Here, a comparison table shows FPO versus individual farmer outcomes. For market access, an individual farmer is limited to the local APMC as a price-taker, while an FPO member has multiple buyers including exporters and direct retail, with price negotiation possible. For input purchase, FPO members get bulk purchase prices 10 to 20 percent lower on fertiliser, seeds, and pesticides. For credit access, FPO members get FPO-level credit with NABARD equity grant and guarantee, compared to an individual loan requiring full collateral. The Agri Lens box describes Karnataka's tomato FPOs in Kolar and Chikkaballapur districts, where individual farmers often receive distress prices of just 1 to 5 rupees per kilogram when the local market is flooded, but Kolar FPOs have built sorting and grading units connected to direct buyers, reducing the price crash. The Did You Know box explains SFAC, the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium, established in 1994 under the Ministry of Agriculture, which provides equity grants, credit guarantees, and facilitates market linkages with APEDA for exports. A field dialogue then begins, with ten jowar farmers from three villages asking the AO about forming a group to sell directly to a flour mill.
188: On this page, the AO confirms that with 10 members, the farmers can register as a Producer Company under the Companies Act, though for practical FPO operation, 50 to 100 members would give meaningful volume, and SFAC's Cluster Based Business Organisation can help with registration, governance, and finding buyers. The AO explains that under the central scheme for 10,000 FPOs, each registered FPO gets up to 18 lakh rupees as grant over 3 years, plus equity grant for working capital and credit guarantee from NABARD, and the scheme also covers the cost of a business expert for the first 3 years. Now, section 5.7 begins, covering Minimum Support Price, or MSP, price policy, and the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices. MSP is the price at which the Government of India commits to purchase crops from farmers if market prices fall below this level, acting as a price floor guaranteeing farmers recover at least the cost of production. The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices, or CACP, is the statutory body that recommends MSPs to the Government of India, established in 1965 under the Ministry of Agriculture, analysing cost of production, market prices, and demand-supply balance. The Union Cabinet, not CACP alone, takes the final decision on MSP announcement.
189: Let us understand the MSP mechanism key facts. MSP is the government-guaranteed floor price for specified crops, recommended by CACP, established in 1965 as a statutory advisory body to the Cabinet. MSP is announced for 23 crops: 14 kharif, 6 rabi, and 2 other crops, namely sugarcane, jute, and copra. Key kharif crops include paddy, jowar, bajra, maize, moong, urad, groundnut, soybean, and cotton. Key rabi crops include wheat, barley, gram, masur, rapeseed or mustard, and safflower. The procurement agency is the Food Corporation of India, or FCI, for rice and wheat, NAFED for pulses and oilseeds, and state agencies for state-specific crops. In Karnataka, the state operates Minimum Support Price procurement through the Karnataka Food and Civil Supplies Corporation, or KFCSC, for paddy, and NAFED for jowar, bajra, and pulses. Now, students, let us understand the cost concepts in MSP: A2, A2 plus FL, and C2. A2 cost includes all paid-out costs incurred by the farmer, such as seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation charges, and hired labour and machinery, representing actual cash expense. A2 plus FL cost adds the imputed value of unpaid family labour to A2, assigning a notional wage at market rates.
190: On this page, we learn about C2 cost, which is A2 plus FL plus imputed interest on owned capital such as machinery and land, and rent on owned land. C2 is the most comprehensive cost concept, including the opportunity cost of the farmer's own capital and land. A comparison table gives example figures per quintal of paddy: A2 costs 800 to 1,000 rupees and is the minimum basis but does not reflect full cost of farming. A2 plus FL costs 1,100 to 1,300 rupees, more realistic since it includes unpaid family labour contribution. C2 costs 1,500 to 1,800 rupees, the most comprehensive, and the Swaminathan Commission recommended 50 percent above C2 as MSP. The Swaminathan Commission, formally the National Commission on Farmers, 2004 to 06, recommended that MSP should be set at 50 percent above C2 cost, meaning MSP equals C2 times 1.5. However, the 2018-19 Union Budget announced that MSP for kharif crops would be fixed at 1.5 times A2 plus FL cost, not C2, creating controversy among farmer organisations who argued the C2-based MSP would be substantially higher.
191: Watch out for this important distinction: the government announced MSP at 150 percent of cost of production in 2018, but this was 150 percent of A2 plus FL, not 150 percent of C2. C2 is higher than A2 plus FL because C2 includes land rent and capital interest, so if C2 were used, MSP would be significantly higher. This A2 plus FL versus C2 distinction is a medium-level trap question in PSC and IAS exams. Remember, Swaminathan recommended C2 as the base, but the Government uses A2 plus FL. Here's the memory trick: A2 is actual paid-out cash you spend, A2 plus FL adds unpaid family work with a notional value, and C2 is the comprehensive cost adding capital interest and land rent, with each level adding a broader cost. Now, section 5.7a begins, covering PMKSY, the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana, and its four components. PMKSY was launched in 2015 by merging three existing irrigation programmes into a single comprehensive water-use scheme. Its core objective is captured in the slogans Har Khet Ko Pani, meaning water to every field, and More Crop Per Drop, meaning water-use efficiency. The first component, AIBP, the Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme, focuses on completing long-pending major and medium irrigation projects, relevant to Karnataka's Upper Bhadra Project and Yettinahole diversion.
192: Let us continue with the remaining PMKSY components. The second component, PMKSY-HKKP, or Har Khet Ko Pani, expands cultivable area under irrigation by creating new water sources and strengthening the distribution network of field channels, extending irrigation to uncovered villages in North Karnataka, particularly field channel repair in Raichur and Yadgir districts. The third component, PMKSY-PDMC, or Per Drop More Crop, promotes micro-irrigation through drip and sprinkler systems for water-use efficiency and precision irrigation, relevant to Karnataka's drip adoption in sugarcane, tomato, and pomegranate, with PDMC subsidy for drip irrigation in water-scarce districts. The fourth component, Watershed, is the Integrated Watershed Management Programme, focusing on soil and water conservation, groundwater recharge, and a participatory approach, relevant to comprehensive watershed programmes in Kolar, Tumkur, and Chitradurga drought-prone belts, where the AO coordinates farm-level water harvesting. For the AO examination, these four components need to be memorised with their names and focuses: AIBP for major irrigation project completion, HKKP for extending irrigation coverage, PDMC for efficiency through micro-irrigation, and Watershed for soil and water conservation, all funded under PMKSY as a unified scheme.
193: On this page, we learn Watershed development under PMKSY covers the rain-fed hill areas of Malnad and the plateau belt in Karnataka. The Agri Lens box explains that the Per Drop More Crop component is most relevant for the Agricultural Officer's daily advisory work: when visiting a farmer growing sugarcane with flood irrigation consuming 1,800 to 2,000 millimetres of water per season, the AO can demonstrate that drip irrigation for sugarcane consumes only 900 to 1,100 millimetres, nearly 40 percent water saving, while increasing yield. PMKSY-PDMC provides a subsidy of 55 percent for small and marginal farmers and 45 percent for others on drip system purchase. Remember, PMKSY has 4 components: AIBP for major projects, HKKP for field extension and coverage, PDMC for drip and sprinkler efficiency, and Watershed for soil and water conservation. The launch year is 2015, and PMKSY replaced AIBP, IWMP, and On-Farm Water Management as three predecessor schemes merged into one. Now, section 5.8 begins, covering Jal Jeevan Mission and Farmer Social Security Schemes. Jal Jeevan Mission, or JJM, was launched on 15 August 2019, with the objective of providing safe and adequate drinking water through individual household tap connections, called Har Ghar Jal, to every rural household in India by 2024, implemented under the Ministry of Jal Shakti.
194: Let us understand Jal Jeevan Mission's key facts further. The target is Functional Household Tap Connections, or FHTC, to every rural household, covering 19.35 crore rural households in India. The Ministry is Jal Shakti, formed by merging the Ministry of Water Resources and the Ministry of Drinking Water and Sanitation. The budget is 3.60 lakh crore rupees, the largest single rural infrastructure investment at launch. In Karnataka, progress has covered over 90 percent of rural households with functional household tap connections, as of 2024-25. The relevance for the AO lies in safe drinking water improving rural health, reducing workday loss, and improving farm productivity, with JJM Gram Panchayat water supply committees coordinating with the AO for land use around water sources. On water quality, JJM includes testing for arsenic, fluoride, and nitrate, and the AO may advise on fertiliser management to reduce nitrate contamination in groundwater. Karnataka's Kalaburagi and Yadgir districts receive particular focus given historical fluoride contamination. Now, students, we move to Farmer Social Security Schemes: PMJJBY, PMSBY, and PM-SYM. These three central schemes provide life insurance, accident insurance, and pension to unorganised sector workers, including farmers, and the Agricultural Officer helps eligible farm families access them.
195: On this page, let us understand the three key farmer social security schemes. First, PMJJBY, Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, provides life insurance for ages 18 to 50 with a bank account. It covers death from any cause, has an annual premium of Rs.436 auto debited from the bank account, and gives a benefit of Rs.2 lakh on death. The AO helps farmers link their bank account and enrol, with the premium auto deducted from KCC or savings account. Second, PMSBY, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana, provides accident insurance for ages 18 to 70, with a very low premium of just Rs.20 per year, auto debited. It gives Rs.2 lakh for accidental death or total disability, and Rs.1 lakh for partial disability. This scheme has a very low premium, affordable for all farmers, and the AO enrols farmers during RSK visits. Third, PM-SYM, Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-Dhan for unorganised workers, or PM Kisan Maan Dhan for farmers, provides pension for unorganised workers and small farmers aged 18 to 40. It is matched by the government and gives Rs.3,000 per month pension at age 60. The AO registers small and marginal farmers who do not file income tax returns for this scheme.
196: Now, students, let us continue with these three schemes together. They cover the major risks faced by a farming family, death from illness under PMJJBY, death or disability from accident under PMSBY, and old age income security under PM-KMY or PM-SYM. The premiums are remarkably low, just Rs.436 per year for PMJJBY and only Rs.20 per year for PMSBY, making these accessible to even the most economically marginal farm families. The Agricultural Officer's role is awareness, enrolment facilitation, and claim assistance. Here is an important exam watch out. PMJJBY and PMSBY are often confused. PMJJBY is life insurance, covering death from any cause, giving Rs.2 lakh benefit. PMSBY is accident insurance, covering only accidental death or disability, giving Rs.2 lakh for full disability and Rs.1 lakh for partial. Remember, PMJJBY covers all deaths, while PMSBY covers only accidental events. Also remember, PMSBY at just Rs.20 per year, less than two rupees a month, is one of the most affordable insurance products anywhere in the world, yet it provides Rs.2 lakh accident death cover. In Karnataka, agricultural accidents like tractor rollovers, pesticide poisoning, and falls from trees make this scheme very important for farm families.
197: Let us understand this quick checkpoint and revision page. The checkpoint asks students to recall the annual premium for PMSBY and its maximum benefit on accidental death, and to distinguish the coverage between PMJJBY and PMSBY. Now, moving to the Key Facts Revision Reference table, this is an important summary for quick revision. PM-Kisan was launched in February 2019, with the first instalment backdated to December 2018, giving Rs.6,000 per year in three instalments of Rs.2,000, transferred through direct benefit transfer to Aadhaar linked accounts. Excluded from PM-Kisan are income tax payers, government servants, constitutional post holders, and professionals. PMFBY, the crop insurance scheme, was launched in 2016 replacing NAIS, with premium rates of 2 percent for kharif crops, 1.5 percent for rabi crops, and 5 percent for commercial and horticulture crops. PMFBY uses yield based triggers from Crop Cutting Experiments data, while RWBCIS uses weather based triggers from Automatic Weather Stations. MGNREGS, enacted in 2005 and implemented in 2006, guarantees 100 days of employment per household per year, creating durable rural assets. RKVY, from 2007, provides flexible funds for agriculture infrastructure. The Soil Health Card, launched in 2015, tests soil every two years across 14 parameters. eNAM, from 2016, is the electronic National Agriculture Market linking APMCs for online price discovery. PMGSY, from 2000, provides all weather rural roads.
198: On this page, we continue the Key Facts Revision Reference table with more important schemes. NHM and MIDH, from 2005, promote horticulture development with subsidy for orchards, protected cultivation, and cold chain. The Kisan Credit Card, from 1998 to 99, was designed by NABARD as a revolving crop loan with 4 percent effective interest rate for timely repayment. NABARD itself was established on 12 July 1982, based on the Shivaraman Committee recommendation, as the apex agricultural credit institution headquartered in Mumbai. PACS in Karnataka number over 5,000, functioning as village level cooperative credit societies for fertiliser distribution. The interest subvention on crop loans is 2 percent central subvention plus 3 percent incentive for prompt repayment, giving an effective 4 percent rate on crop loans up to Rs.3 lakh. PM-KMY or PM-SYM, from 2019, gives pension for farmers and unorganised workers aged 18 to 40, providing Rs.3,000 per month pension at age 60. Raitha Siri is Karnataka's PMFBY top up scheme, and Krishi Bhagya targets farm ponds and micro irrigation for the 67 percent rainfed area. Raitha Sampark Kendra is Karnataka's single window agri service centre at hobli or taluk level. The FPO scheme from 2020 aims for 10,000 FPOs in 5 years with Rs.18 lakh grant per FPO, registered as a Producer Company under Companies Act 2013 with a minimum of 10 members. CACP, from 1965, recommends MSP to the Cabinet for 23 crops. Remember the MSP cost concepts, A2 means paid out costs, A2 plus FL adds family labour, and C2 is the most comprehensive, adding capital interest and land rent.
199: Let us finish this important revision table. Government policy announces MSP at 1.5 times A2 plus FL, not C2, and this difference is frequently tested in exams. PMKSY, launched in 2015, has four components, AIBP for major projects, HKKP for field coverage, PDMC for drip and sprinkler irrigation, and Watershed development. The PMKSY slogans to remember are Har Khet Ko Pani, meaning water to every field, for HKKP, and More Crop Per Drop, meaning micro irrigation efficiency, for PDMC. The Jal Jeevan Mission, from 15 August 2019, aims for Har Ghar Jal, meaning functional household tap connections to every rural household, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, with an outlay of Rs.3.60 lakh crore. We again see PMJJBY as life insurance at Rs.436 per year for Rs.2 lakh on death from any cause, ages 18 to 50, and PMSBY as accident insurance at Rs.20 per year for Rs.2 lakh on accidental death or full disability, and Rs.1 lakh for partial, ages 18 to 70. Remember, PMJJBY covers any death while PMSBY covers only accidental events. Karnataka Raitha Suraksha is state compensation for crop losses from natural calamities not covered under PMFBY. Scale of Finance is set by the District Level Technical Committee, deciding crop wise loan limits for KCC. The Hani survey, or Girdavari, is the crop loss assessment survey conducted by the AO after a natural calamity, forming the basis for compensation under state schemes.
200: Here, students, we have a Mind Map summarizing the entire unit on Rural Development and Schemes. At the centre is Rural Development and Schemes, Unit 5, branching into eight major categories. First, PM-Kisan, covering its February 2019 launch, Rs.6,000 per year, and exclusions.
